## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{100}{0}{0}{0}{0}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why can a model with a tenth of the token price make an agent cost more for every task it finishes?_

A team that prices an agent from its token bill misses much of what it buys. Each accepted result carries model calls, sandbox time, tool fees, assessment, and any human work, together with the spending on tasks that never passed. A cheaper model can require more turns and leave more work unresolved; a faster model barely shortens a trajectory whose time goes to tests and tool waits. Economics therefore connects model choice, caching, reasoning budgets, routing, and capacity to the outcome the service is meant to deliver. Lower cost matters within declared acceptance and deadline constraints, and a deadline benefit can justify higher spending. Horizon sets how many steps require funding, state affects what each step must retain and read, and authority determines which effects need mediation and assessment, making the cost of closure a property of the whole trajectory.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Calculate cohort cost per accepted task while distinguishing attempt costs, human outcomes, and unsettled liabilities
- Evaluate caching, compaction, and reasoning or retry purchases under explicit billing and acceptance assumptions
- Diagnose critical-path investments using execution dependencies, component costs, and available serving capacity
- Evaluate model cascades under a common acceptance contract, including assessment costs and false-accept risk
- Size resource occupancy and compare provisioning choices under declared workload, quota, and queueing assumptions
- Design atomic budget reservations that preserve spending bounds across concurrent work and late settlement
- Select an architecture using declared acceptance, cost, latency, and authority constraints rather than agent count

:::

## Cost per Accepted Task {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-accounting}

The repair agent (\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}) can spend less on each model call and more on each accepted repair. The cheaper calls may require additional turns, each holding a sandbox and invoking tools, and more tickets may remain unresolved after assessment. The token discount is real, but it applies to only part of the account. The engineering comparison joins spending to the same task outcomes whose evidence @sec-vol3-evaluation established.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_hsa.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with all three axes, Horizon, State, and Authority, highlighted."}

*Horizon, state, and authority each set the closure a task must pay for.*
:::

@Sec-vol3-intro introduced cost per accepted task as one of the book's two quantitative fundamentals: the expected cost of an attempt divided by the probability that the attempt is accepted. That ratio is the quantity this chapter develops. Its numerator must hold every charge an attempt incurs, its denominator must count only outcomes accepted under one declared contract, and each lever the runtime controls (reuse, retries, acceleration, routing, capacity, and delegation) is worth buying only if it lowers the ratio or buys a deadline the objective values. An agent evaluation that reports accuracy without cost cannot show this ratio, which is why cost-controlled evaluation reports the two jointly and compares designs on both [@kapoor2024agents].

Acceptance is scoped to one declared contract, checker, and environment. Every comparison in this chapter is a matched comparison, holding those three and the available resource ceilings fixed while the policy changes; changing the contract while changing models confounds the result. The account also needs a population and a cutoff, which fix the initiated tasks it covers, the results accepted by the cutoff, and the operations, assessments, or charges still pending.

### From an attempt to a task account

Across an attempt of $K$ turns, the runtime incurs model charges and pays for the environment in which proposed actions execute. Assessment, cleanup, and human work may continue after the final model call. A useful decomposition is

$$C_{\text{attempt}} = \sum_{k=1}^K \left(C_{\text{in},k}+C_{\text{out},k}+C_{\text{tools},k}+C_{\text{sandbox},k}\right)+C_{\text{verify}}+C_{\text{cleanup}}+C_{\text{human}}+C_{\text{runtime}}.$$

The input and output terms use the applicable billing categories, including any cached-input charges. The tool term covers external service fees; the sandbox term covers its charged lifetime, including waits when the resource remains allocated. Verification covers assessment not already charged elsewhere. Cleanup includes required release or compensation work, and the human term includes the declared review or handling boundary. Runtime cost includes orchestration and allocated shared infrastructure overhead. Each charge belongs in exactly one category; a test billed as sandbox execution must not also appear as a second verification charge for that same resource.

::: {#dfn-whole-trajectory-cost .callout-definition title="Whole-trajectory cost"}

***Whole-trajectory cost***\index{Whole-trajectory cost!definition} is the total cost attributed to one execution attempt across its model calls, environment, assessment, and required finalization within a declared accounting boundary.

1. **Significance**: It is the numerator of cost per accepted task, $C_{\text{eff}}$, and it holds every charge a per-token price omits: sandbox holding, tools, assessment, cleanup, and human work, on attempts that fail as fully as on attempts that pass.
2. **Distinction**: It prices one attempt. Cost per accepted task also charges the other attempts and tasks in the counted population to the accepted outcomes.
3. **Common pitfall**: Ending the account when a local agent stops even though remote operations, cleanup, or human handling still incur charges.

:::

An initiated task can contain several attempts or delegated branches. Its **task account**\index{Task account!definition}, $C_{\text{task},i}$, includes all of that work once, together with the task's share of capacity and operations costs; a failed or canceled branch stays in the account after its output is discarded. A reserved amount backs authorized work or possible liability without yet being a charge, and it stays reserved while the obligations it covers remain open. A report at an intermediate cutoff therefore separates settled spending from **outstanding liability**\index{Outstanding liability!definition}, the reserved amount still backing unsettled operations, and treats the settled subtotal as a floor on the task's price.

### Charging all work to accepted outcomes

For a finite cohort of $N$ initiated tasks with completed accounting, let $N_{\text{acc}}$ be the number of distinct tasks accepted under the declared contract. Repeated successful attempts at the same task do not create additional accepted tasks. For $N_{\text{acc}}>0$,

$$C_{\text{eff}}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}C_{\text{task},i}}{N_{\text{acc}}}. $$

The numerator includes every initiated task, accepted or not. When none is accepted, the ratio has no finite value, and the report gives the spending and the zero directly. When outcomes or charges are pending, the report gives the cutoff and those statuses beside any provisional ratio. A missing assessment is pending rather than failed, and a late charge can move the ratio without changing any artifact.

::: {#dfn-18-cost-per-accepted-task .callout-definition title="Cohort cost per accepted task"}

***Cohort cost per accepted task***\index{Cost per accepted task!cohort definition} is the total cost of every initiated task in a cohort, within a declared accounting boundary, divided by the number of distinct tasks accepted under one declared contract.

1. **Significance**: It is the measurable form of the volume's economic fundamental $C_{\text{eff}}$ from @sec-vol3-intro-horizon-arithmetic. Acceptance divides every term of the account, so a change in acceptance moves the whole bill, while a token discount moves only the model's share of it.
2. **Distinction**: Whole-trajectory cost prices one attempt; cost per accepted task charges failed, canceled, and unassessed attempts to the accepted outcomes.
3. **Common pitfall**: Averaging the cost of successful trajectories, which omits the nonaccepted tasks that each accepted task also pays for.

:::

For a fully classified cohort, write the acceptance fraction as $\alpha=N_{\text{acc}}/N$. Let $C_{\text{succ}}$ be the mean total task cost among accepted tasks and $C_{\text{fail}}$ the mean among nonaccepted tasks, including failed and canceled tasks. When both groups are nonempty, separating the numerator gives

$$C_{\text{eff}}=C_{\text{succ}}+\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}C_{\text{fail}}.$$

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_economics_rejected_per_accepted_margin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Curve of rejected tasks per accepted task falling steeply as acceptance rises. A red dot at low acceptance is labeled 3 and a green dot at high acceptance is labeled 0.33."}

*Each accepted task carries the rejected ones, and that load explodes as acceptance falls.*
:::

The multiplier $(1-\alpha)/\alpha$ counts nonaccepted tasks per accepted task. It is a cohort identity, not an assumption that retries eventually solve every ticket, and it grows without bound as acceptance falls. Whether a token discount survives it depends on both groups' costs, which is why no single acceptance threshold decides the question; the next calculation prices one case.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-token-price
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE TOKEN-PRICE FALLACY IN A FINITE BUG-REPAIR COHORT (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Goal: Compare total spend per accepted task, with and without human triage.
# │ Show: Model and attempt costs, cohort costs, and accepted-task ratios.
# │ How:  One bounded attempt per ticket; all outcomes and charges settled.
# │ Note: Hypothetical prices and counts, not a provider schedule or experiment.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_usd, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent

class TokenPriceFallacy:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    tickets = 100
    a_accepted, b_accepted = 75, 25
    a_in, a_out = 3.00, 15.00  # scenario USD per million tokens
    b_in, b_out = 0.30, 1.20
    a_turns, b_turns = 4, 7
    a_ctx, a_gen = 16_000, 800  # scenario tokens per turn
    b_ctx, b_gen = 28_000, 1_200
    c_env = 0.03  # scenario USD per turn, all tool/sandbox holding charges
    c_verify = 0.05  # scenario USD per attempt, additional assessment
    c_human = 10.00  # scenario USD per rejected attempt, triage only

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    a_model = a_turns * (a_ctx * a_in + a_gen * a_out) / 1e6
    b_model = b_turns * (b_ctx * b_in + b_gen * b_out) / 1e6
    a_attempt = a_model + a_turns * c_env + c_verify
    b_attempt = b_model + b_turns * c_env + c_verify
    a_total, b_total = tickets * a_attempt, tickets * b_attempt
    a_rejected, b_rejected = tickets - a_accepted, tickets - b_accepted
    a_total_h = a_total + a_rejected * c_human
    b_total_h = b_total + b_rejected * c_human
    a_eff, b_eff = a_total / a_accepted, b_total / b_accepted
    a_eff_h, b_eff_h = a_total_h / a_accepted, b_total_h / b_accepted
    eff_ratio, eff_h_ratio = b_eff / a_eff, b_eff_h / a_eff_h
    a_fail_per_acc, b_fail_per_acc = a_rejected / a_accepted, b_rejected / b_accepted
    model_cut = 1 - b_model / a_model  # token-charge reduction per attempt
    attempt_cut = 1 - b_attempt / a_attempt  # all-in reduction per attempt
    needed_cut = 1 - b_accepted / a_accepted  # attempt cut that would tie per accepted task

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < b_accepted < a_accepted < tickets, "Both cohorts need accepted and rejected tasks")
    check(a_accepted + a_rejected == tickets and b_accepted + b_rejected == tickets, "Every initiated ticket must have a declared outcome")
    check(b_model < a_model and b_attempt < a_attempt, "Cheap model must cost less per attempt")
    check(b_eff > a_eff and eff_h_ratio > eff_ratio, "Acceptance and triage reverse the ranking")
    check(abs(a_total_h - a_total - a_rejected * c_human) < 1e-9, "Triage cost must be included exactly once")
    check(attempt_cut < needed_cut < model_cut, "Token cut exceeds the tie point; the all-in cut falls short")
    check(abs(eff_ratio - (1 - attempt_cut) / (1 - needed_cut)) < 1e-9, "Ratio of attempt costs over ratio of acceptances")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    tickets_str = fmt_int(tickets)
    a_accepted_str, b_accepted_str = fmt_int(a_accepted), fmt_int(b_accepted)
    a_rejected_str, b_rejected_str = fmt_int(a_rejected), fmt_int(b_rejected)
    a_in_str, a_out_str = fmt_usd(a_in, precision=0), fmt_usd(a_out, precision=0)
    b_in_str, b_out_str = fmt_usd(b_in, precision=2), fmt_usd(b_out, precision=2)
    a_turns_str, b_turns_str = fmt_int(a_turns), fmt_int(b_turns)
    a_ctx_str, a_gen_str = fmt_int(a_ctx), fmt_int(a_gen)
    b_ctx_str, b_gen_str = fmt_int(b_ctx), fmt_int(b_gen)
    c_env_str, c_verify_str = fmt_usd(c_env, precision=2), fmt_usd(c_verify, precision=2)
    c_human_str = fmt_usd(c_human, precision=0)
    a_model_str, b_model_str = fmt_usd(a_model, precision=3), fmt_usd(b_model, precision=3)
    a_attempt_str, b_attempt_str = fmt_usd(a_attempt, precision=3), fmt_usd(b_attempt, precision=3)
    a_total_str, b_total_str = fmt_usd(a_total, precision=0), fmt_usd(b_total, precision=3)
    a_total_h_str, b_total_h_str = fmt_usd(a_total_h, precision=0), fmt_usd(b_total_h, precision=3)
    a_eff_str, b_eff_str = fmt_usd(a_eff, precision=2), fmt_usd(b_eff, precision=2)
    a_eff_h_str, b_eff_h_str = fmt_usd(a_eff_h, precision=2), fmt_usd(b_eff_h, precision=2)
    eff_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(eff_ratio, precision=1)
    eff_h_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(eff_h_ratio, precision=1)
    a_fail_per_acc_str, b_fail_per_acc_str = fmt(a_fail_per_acc, precision=2), fmt(b_fail_per_acc, precision=0)
    model_cut_str = fmt_percent(model_cut, precision=1)
    attempt_cut_str = fmt_percent(attempt_cut, precision=1)
    needed_cut_str = fmt_percent(needed_cut, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-18-the-token-price-fallacy-in-automated .callout-notebook title="The token-price fallacy in automated bug repair"}

**Problem:** Two hypothetical configurations each process the same `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.tickets_str` tickets, with one bounded attempt per ticket and the same acceptance contract. Every attempt, rejected or not, uses the fixed per-attempt usage below, and all outcomes and charges are settled at the cutoff. The environment charge covers tool use, sandbox holding, and cleanup; the assessment charge covers checking not billed as sandbox time, together with allocated runtime overhead. Which configuration costs less per accepted repair?

| Parameter                               | Frontier configuration                                                          | Low-token-price configuration                                                   |
|:----------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Input / output price per million tokens | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_in_str` / `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_out_str`  | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_in_str` / `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_out_str`  |
| Turns per attempt                       | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_turns_str`                                        | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_turns_str`                                        |
| Input / output tokens per turn          | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_ctx_str` / `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_gen_str` | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_ctx_str` / `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_gen_str` |
| Accepted tickets                        | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_accepted_str`                                     | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_accepted_str`                                     |
| Environment cost per turn               | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.c_env_str`                                          | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.c_env_str`                                          |
| Additional assessment per attempt       | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.c_verify_str`                                       | `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.c_verify_str`                                       |

: **Illustrative Bug-Repair Cohort**: Assumed prices, usage, and accepted counts for two configurations; these are arithmetic inputs, not observed measurements. {#tbl-vol3-token-price-fallacy}

**Math:** Applying the rates and usage in @tbl-vol3-token-price-fallacy gives model charges per attempt of `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_model_str` and `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_model_str`. Adding the other charges gives `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_attempt_str` and `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_attempt_str`, respectively. The complete cohorts therefore cost `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_total_str` and `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_total_str`. Dividing each total by its accepted count gives `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_eff_str` and `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_eff_str` per accepted repair. The lower-token-price configuration costs less per attempt but `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.eff_ratio_mult_str` as much per accepted task.

Now expand both accounting boundaries to include `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.c_human_str` of engineer triage for each rejected attempt. The frontier configuration has `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_rejected_str` rejected tickets and the other has `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_rejected_str`. Total costs become `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_total_h_str` and `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_total_h_str`; costs per accepted task become `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_eff_h_str` and `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_eff_h_str`, a ratio of `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.eff_h_ratio_mult_str`. Triage adds no accepted repairs; if engineers also completed tickets, that combined service would need its own named account.

**Systems insight:** With one attempt per ticket, a cheaper configuration wins only if its attempt cost falls by more than its acceptance does. Here acceptance falls by `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.needed_cut_str` percent, so the low-price configuration needed attempts at least that much cheaper. Its token charges fall by `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.model_cut_str` percent, but its all-in attempt cost falls by only `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.attempt_cut_str` percent, because its extra turns each pay the environment charge. Each of its accepted repairs also carries `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.b_fail_per_acc_str` rejected attempts, against `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.a_fail_per_acc_str` for the frontier configuration, so every charge that scales with rejections, such as triage, widens the gap.

:::

::: {#psp-18-reading-cost-per-accepted .callout-perspective title="Reading a cost-per-accepted-task number"}

A cost per accepted task is a ratio of two totals over one cohort and one cutoff. It is not the mean of per-task costs, and in a small cohort it is not an unbiased estimate of the planning ratio $\mathbb{E}[C_{\text{attempt}}]/p_{\text{acc}}$. Read it together with the numbers that share its cohort and cutoff: the accepted count and its uncertainty, total cost, latency, pending outcomes, and outstanding liability. A number reported without them cannot be compared with another policy's.

A matched comparison fixes the contract and the resource ceilings, not the amount spent. A policy may spend more to meet a deadline or cover more tasks when the declared objective values that. The reciprocal, accepted tasks per dollar, is **goodput per dollar**\index{Goodput per dollar!definition}; it counts the same outcomes and charges the same work. In either direction, acceptance is evidence under the contract's scope, not proof that the accepted artifact has no latent defect (@sec-vol3-evaluation-grading).

:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}

↩ Acceptance evidence, matched comparisons, and incomplete outcomes are established in @sec-vol3-evaluation.

:::

The account also names the next purchase to examine. The account's largest term differs by workload, and @sec-vol3-agent-economics-synthesis prices all four lighthouse workloads once the chapter's levers are in hand. For the repair agent, repeated input is a large share of model charges: prefix reuse and compaction change what the runtime pays to carry that context, while reasoning and retry policies change how many calls it buys.

## Caching and Reasoning Budgets {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-caching}

An input token can appear in many calls without its attention state being recomputed each time, and reused state is cheaper without being free. @Sec-vol3-context-engineering and @sec-vol3-kv-cache established when reuse is valid; this section prices it, then asks whether changing the context or purchasing additional attempts lowers cost per accepted task under the same contract.

### Economic valuation of prefix cache hits

Separate the logical input from the work performed and the amount billed. A service may retain compatible KV state between calls even when the client supplies the full logical transcript again.[^fn-prefix-reuse-billing] Over a trajectory of $K$ calls, let $L_t$ be the logical input length on call $t$, $L_{\mathrm{hit},t}$ its eligible cached prefix, and $O_t$ its billed output length. For a declared tariff with per-token prices $p_{\mathrm{in}}$, $p_{\mathrm{cache}}$, and $p_{\mathrm{out}}$, the token charge is

$$
C_{\mathrm{session}}=\sum_{t=1}^{K}\left[p_{\mathrm{in}}(L_t-L_{\mathrm{hit},t})+p_{\mathrm{cache}}L_{\mathrm{hit},t}+p_{\mathrm{out}}O_t\right].
$$ {#eq-vol3-agent-economics-session-bill}

[^fn-prefix-reuse-billing]: **Prefix Reuse**: Serving systems made cross-request reuse practical by storing attention state in blocks that requests with a common prefix can share [@kwon2023], and by indexing retained state in a radix tree so a later call can find its longest cached prefix [@zheng2024sglang]. A cached-input price is the billing face of that mechanism, so it inherits the mechanism's condition: only an exactly matching prefix that is still resident is discounted.

Real tariffs add categories to this model, such as cache-write charges, retention charges, and minimum eligible lengths. In an append-only transcript, each call's input is the previous call's input plus the tokens generated and observed on the previous turn. If the first prompt has $L_0$ tokens and each turn appends exactly $\Delta L$, total logical input is

$$
L_{\mathrm{tot}}=K L_0+\Delta L\frac{K(K-1)}{2}.
$$

Under ideal prefix reuse, the first prompt and each appended increment are charged as fresh input once: $L_{\mathrm{fresh}}=L_0+(K-1)\Delta L$. The input charge is therefore $p_{\mathrm{in}}L_{\mathrm{fresh}}+p_{\mathrm{cache}}(L_{\mathrm{tot}}-L_{\mathrm{fresh}})$. For positive $p_{\mathrm{cache}}$ and $\Delta L$, the quadratic term remains; caching lowers its coefficient to the cached rate rather than removing it. These equations count billed input; the memory that holds reusable state is the subject of @sec-vol3-kv-cache.

The cache must match the delivered token prefix and the relevant model, configuration, and isolation conditions (principle \ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}). Reuse ends at the first changed token, and routing, eviction, and long tool waits lower the realized hit rate, so the account prices observed eligible hits under the actual service contract.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-prefix-cache
#| echo: false
#| output: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PRICE REUSED INPUT AND COMPACTION (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-18-prefix-cache-dollars and @nbk-vol3-compaction-crossing.
# │ Goal: Price logical input and find the first paying compaction horizon.
# │ Show: Cache bill, summary/rebuild cost, and adjacent integer horizons.
# │ How: Declared ideal-reuse tariff; compaction causes a complete cache miss.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from math import ceil
from mlsysim import USD
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_usd, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent

class PrefixCacheCost:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Hypothetical tariff and fixed trajectory) ────────────────
    turns, s0, delta, k_turn = 30, 8_000, 1_500, 200
    p_in, p_out = 3 * USD, 15 * USD  # per million tokens
    cached_share = 0.10
    compact_turn, compact_to, summary_out = 16, 12_000, 1_500

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Bills and incremental compaction cost) ────────────────
    sent = turns * s0 + delta * turns * (turns - 1) // 2
    fresh = s0 + delta * (turns - 1)
    in_nocache = sent * p_in / 1_000_000
    in_cache = (fresh + cached_share * (sent - fresh)) * p_in / 1_000_000
    out_cost = turns * k_turn * p_out / 1_000_000
    total_nocache, total_cache = in_nocache + out_cost, in_cache + out_cost
    cache_ratio = (total_nocache / total_cache).magnitude
    ctx_at = s0 + (compact_turn - 1) * delta
    rest = turns - compact_turn + 1
    first_keep = (delta + (ctx_at - delta) * cached_share) * p_in / 1_000_000
    first_comp = compact_to * p_in / 1_000_000
    summary_cost = first_keep + summary_out * p_out / 1_000_000
    upfront = summary_cost + first_comp - first_keep
    per_turn_saving = (ctx_at - compact_to) * cached_share * p_in / 1_000_000
    breakeven_turns = 1 + ceil((upfront / per_turn_saving).magnitude)
    keep_sum = rest * ctx_at + delta * rest * (rest - 1) // 2
    keep_cost = (rest * delta + cached_share * (keep_sum - rest * delta)) * p_in / 1_000_000
    comp_sum = rest * compact_to + delta * rest * (rest - 1) // 2
    comp_fresh = compact_to + (rest - 1) * delta
    comp_cost = (comp_fresh + cached_share * (comp_sum - comp_fresh)) * p_in / 1_000_000
    comp_total = comp_cost + summary_cost
    gap_before = upfront - (breakeven_turns - 2) * per_turn_saving
    saving_at = (breakeven_turns - 1) * per_turn_saving - upfront
    hit_drop = 0.10  # scenario: share of the eligible prefix that misses
    miss_cost = hit_drop * (sent - fresh) * (1 - cached_share) * p_in / 1_000_000
    miss_pct = (miss_cost / total_cache).magnitude
    # upfront does not depend on the cached rate; the per-call saving scales with it
    breakeven_half = 1 + ceil((upfront / (per_turn_saving / 2)).magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Independent direct sums and integer crossing) ───────────
    direct_keep, direct_comp = 0 * USD, first_comp
    for j in range(rest):
        direct_keep += (delta + cached_share * (ctx_at + j * delta - delta)) * p_in / 1_000_000
        if j > 0:
            direct_comp += (delta + cached_share * (compact_to + (j - 1) * delta)) * p_in / 1_000_000
    check(abs((direct_keep - keep_cost).to(USD).magnitude) < 1e-12, "Keep sum")
    check(abs((direct_comp - comp_cost).to(USD).magnitude) < 1e-12, "Compact sum")
    check(
        abs(((comp_total - keep_cost) - (upfront - (rest - 1) * per_turn_saving)).to(USD).magnitude) < 1e-12,
        "First-turn incremental cost plus later savings",
    )
    check(gap_before > 0 * USD and saving_at >= 0 * USD, "First integer crossing")
    check(breakeven_turns == 12 and comp_total < keep_cost, "Scenario crossing")
    check(breakeven_half > rest >= breakeven_turns, "Halving the cached rate pushes payback past the horizon")
    check(0.3 < miss_pct < 0.6, "A ten-point hit-rate loss is a large share of the cached bill")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    turns_str, s0_str, delta_str = fmt_int(turns), fmt_int(s0), fmt_int(delta)
    k_turn_str = fmt_int(k_turn)
    p_in_str, p_out_str = fmt_usd(p_in, precision=0), fmt_usd(p_out, precision=0)
    cached_pct_str = fmt_percent(cached_share, precision=0)
    sent_str, fresh_str = fmt_int(sent), fmt_int(fresh)
    in_nocache_str, in_cache_str = fmt_usd(in_nocache, precision=3), fmt_usd(in_cache, precision=3)
    out_cost_str = fmt_usd(out_cost, precision=3)
    total_nocache_str, total_cache_str = fmt_usd(total_nocache, precision=3), fmt_usd(total_cache, precision=3)
    cache_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(cache_ratio, precision=1)
    compact_turn_str, ctx_at_str = fmt_int(compact_turn), fmt_int(ctx_at)
    compact_to_str, summary_out_str = fmt_int(compact_to), fmt_int(summary_out)
    rest_str = fmt_int(rest)
    keep_cost_str, comp_cost_str = fmt_usd(keep_cost, precision=5), fmt_usd(comp_cost, precision=5)
    summary_cost_str, comp_total_str = fmt_usd(summary_cost, precision=5), fmt_usd(comp_total, precision=5)
    upfront_str, per_turn_saving_str = fmt_usd(upfront, precision=5), fmt_usd(per_turn_saving, precision=5)
    breakeven_turns_str, before_str = fmt_int(breakeven_turns), fmt_int(breakeven_turns - 1)
    gap_before_str, saving_at_str = fmt_usd(gap_before, precision=5), fmt_usd(saving_at, precision=5)
    hit_drop_str = fmt_percent(hit_drop, precision=0)
    miss_cost_str = fmt_usd(miss_cost, precision=3)
    miss_pct_str = fmt_percent(miss_pct, precision=1)
    half_cached_pct_str = fmt_percent(cached_share / 2, precision=0)
    breakeven_half_str = fmt_int(breakeven_half)
```

::: {#nbk-18-prefix-cache-dollars .callout-notebook title="Pricing an append-only trajectory"}

**Problem**: A hypothetical trajectory runs `{python} PrefixCacheCost.turns_str` turns, beginning with `{python} PrefixCacheCost.s0_str` input tokens and appending `{python} PrefixCacheCost.delta_str` tokens per turn. Each call generates `{python} PrefixCacheCost.k_turn_str` output tokens. The tariff charges `{python} PrefixCacheCost.p_in_str` per million fresh input tokens, `{python} PrefixCacheCost.p_out_str` per million output tokens, and `{python} PrefixCacheCost.cached_pct_str` percent of the fresh-input rate for cached reads, with no separate write or retention fee. How much does ideal prefix reuse reduce this trajectory's token bill?

**Math**: Total logical input is `{python} PrefixCacheCost.sent_str` tokens. With ideal reuse, `{python} PrefixCacheCost.fresh_str` are charged at the fresh-input rate. Input therefore costs `{python} PrefixCacheCost.in_nocache_str` without reuse and `{python} PrefixCacheCost.in_cache_str` with it. Adding the unchanged `{python} PrefixCacheCost.out_cost_str` output charge gives `{python} PrefixCacheCost.total_nocache_str` and `{python} PrefixCacheCost.total_cache_str`, a `{python} PrefixCacheCost.cache_ratio_mult_str` ratio.

**Systems insight**: The hit rate is the knob. Almost all of this trajectory's input is re-read history, so if `{python} PrefixCacheCost.hit_drop_str` percent of the eligible prefix misses, for example because a volatile field sits near the front of the prompt, the bill rises by `{python} PrefixCacheCost.miss_cost_str`, or `{python} PrefixCacheCost.miss_pct_str` percent of the cached total. Reuse changes only the model term of $C_{\text{eff}}$: it lowers the price of carrying context and leaves the delivered inputs, the outputs, and acceptance unchanged.

:::

### The price of compaction

Compaction changes the input itself. Replacing old turns with a summary can preserve a stable system prefix, so a complete cache miss is not inevitable. To expose the economic trade-off, consider a declared complete-miss case: the first compacted call has no reusable prefix, while subsequent calls again reuse their append-only history. Compare it with keeping the original cached context over the same remaining calls, holding future increments and ordinary output costs equal. The comparison prices compaction; whether the summary preserves acceptance is a separate measurement (@sec-vol3-context-engineering).

Let $L$ be the input length at the decision, $M<L$ the compacted length, and $N_{\mathrm{rem}}\ge1$ the remaining ordinary calls, **including the first compacted call**. In this scenario the summary call reads the same cached history, at the same input charge, as the first call on the path that keeps the context, so those two charges cancel in the comparison and the summary adds only its $O_{\mathrm{sum}}$ output tokens. The first compacted ordinary call then reads all $M$ tokens as fresh input. Relative to not compacting, the upfront increment is

$$
U=p_{\mathrm{out}}O_{\mathrm{sum}}+p_{\mathrm{in}}M,
$$

the price of summarizing plus the price of rebuilding the cache. A different summarizer or prefix layout requires its actual charge instead. Each later call saves $s=p_{\mathrm{cache}}(L-M)$ under the equal-growth assumption. Thus

$$
C_{\mathrm{compact}}(N_{\mathrm{rem}})-C_{\mathrm{keep}}(N_{\mathrm{rem}})=U-(N_{\mathrm{rem}}-1)s,
\qquad
N_{\min}=1+\left\lceil\frac{U}{s}\right\rceil
\quad(U>0,\ s>0).
$$

$N_{\min}$ is the **payback horizon**\index{Payback horizon!definition}: the smallest number of remaining calls at which compaction costs no more than keeping the context. If $U\le0$, the first call already pays back; if $s=0$ and $U>0$, compaction never pays for itself in price. Counting the first compacted call separately from the later ones prevents an off-by-one error in the remaining horizon.

::: {#nbk-vol3-compaction-crossing .callout-notebook title="Count the first compacted call"}

**Problem**: In the preceding scenario, compact at turn `{python} PrefixCacheCost.compact_turn_str`, reducing `{python} PrefixCacheCost.ctx_at_str` tokens to `{python} PrefixCacheCost.compact_to_str`. The summary call emits `{python} PrefixCacheCost.summary_out_str` tokens and receives the stated cached-history pricing. There are `{python} PrefixCacheCost.rest_str` ordinary calls left, including the first compacted one. What is the minimum remaining horizon at which compaction costs no more than keeping the context?

**Math**: Keeping the context costs `{python} PrefixCacheCost.keep_cost_str` in remaining input. Compaction costs `{python} PrefixCacheCost.comp_cost_str` in ordinary input plus `{python} PrefixCacheCost.summary_cost_str` for the summary, or `{python} PrefixCacheCost.comp_total_str`. The upfront increment is `{python} PrefixCacheCost.upfront_str`; each later call saves `{python} PrefixCacheCost.per_turn_saving_str`. With `{python} PrefixCacheCost.before_str` calls left, compaction still costs `{python} PrefixCacheCost.gap_before_str` more. With `{python} PrefixCacheCost.breakeven_turns_str` left, it saves `{python} PrefixCacheCost.saving_at_str`.

**Systems insight**: Compaction pays for itself in price only when at least $N_{\min}$ calls remain, and $N_{\min}$ moves inversely with the cached rate: the upfront increment $U$ does not depend on $p_{\mathrm{cache}}$, while the per-call saving $s$ is proportional to it. At a cached rate of `{python} PrefixCacheCost.half_cached_pct_str` percent instead of `{python} PrefixCacheCost.cached_pct_str`, the payback horizon grows to `{python} PrefixCacheCost.breakeven_half_str` calls, more than the `{python} PrefixCacheCost.rest_str` that remain, and the same compaction loses money. The cheaper the cache, the earlier in a trajectory compaction must happen to pay; late compaction is justified by context quality or the model's input limit, and a summary that drops a constraint and lowers acceptance erases any token saving.

:::

### Reasoning and retry budgets

The runtime can also purchase more deliberation within a call or more assessed attempts. A configured reasoning limit is a ceiling; the account prices the realized billed usage and its measured effect on acceptance under the same assessment contract, and it measures latency separately, since extra serial generation lengthens the call.

For a deliberately simple model of **sequential retry**\index{Sequential retry!definition}, which stops at the first accepted attempt, assume every task in the comparison has the same per-attempt acceptance probability $p>0$. Conditional on that task's fixed input and environment, attempts are independent draws from the same configuration, each costing $c$ including assessment and other counted work. Sequential retry stops at the first accepted result or after $k$ attempts. Its acceptance probability is $Q_k=1-(1-p)^k$, and its expected attempt count is $\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-p)^j=Q_k/p$. Consequently, expected spend divided by expected accepted tasks is $(cQ_k/p)/Q_k=c/p$, the introduction's form of cost per accepted task, now derived for a stopping policy: the retry cap sets coverage, and early stopping keeps the price per acceptance at $c/p$.

Launching all $k$ attempts and paying for all of them instead costs $kc/Q_k$ per expected accepted task, provided the same assessment can identify and return an accepted candidate.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-retry-budget
#| echo: false
#| output: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PRICE BOUNDED ATTEMPT POLICIES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-vol3-economics-retry-policies.
# │ Goal: Separate coverage, per-input spend, and cost per accepted task.
# │ Show: Sequential early stop, fully paid batch, and one stronger attempt.
# │ How: Homogeneous conditional iid acceptance and fixed all-in attempt cost.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import USD
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_usd, fmt_percent, fmt_multiple

class RetryBudget:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Independent hypothetical policy comparison) ──────────────
    p_small, p_big, k = 0.30, 0.70, 5
    c_small, c_big = 0.10 * USD, 0.40 * USD

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Expected costs include rejected attempts) ─────────────
    coverage = 1 - (1 - p_small) ** k
    seq_attempts = 0.0
    for j in range(k):
        seq_attempts += (1 - p_small) ** j
    seq_cost, par_cost = c_small * seq_attempts, k * c_small
    seq_per_acc, par_per_acc = seq_cost / coverage, par_cost / coverage
    big_per_acc = c_big / p_big
    batch_premium = k / seq_attempts  # paid batch vs. early stop, same coverage

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Geometric identity and scenario ordering) ───────────────
    check(abs(seq_attempts - coverage / p_small) < 1e-12, "Expected attempts")
    check(abs((seq_per_acc - c_small / p_small).to(USD).magnitude) < 1e-12, "Cost ratio")
    check(coverage > p_big and seq_per_acc < big_per_acc < par_per_acc, "Scenario comparison")
    check(abs(batch_premium - (par_per_acc / seq_per_acc)) < 1e-9, "Batch premium is the attempt ratio")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    p_small_str, p_big_str = fmt(p_small, precision=2), fmt(p_big, precision=2)
    c_small_str, c_big_str = fmt_usd(c_small, precision=2), fmt_usd(c_big, precision=2)
    k_str, coverage_str = fmt_int(k), fmt_percent(coverage, precision=1)
    seq_attempts_str = fmt(seq_attempts, precision=3)
    seq_cost_str, par_cost_str = fmt_usd(seq_cost, precision=3), fmt_usd(par_cost, precision=3)
    seq_per_acc_str = fmt_usd(seq_per_acc, precision=3)
    par_per_acc_str, big_per_acc_str = fmt_usd(par_per_acc, precision=3), fmt_usd(big_per_acc, precision=3)
    p_big_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_big, precision=0)
    batch_premium_mult_str = fmt_multiple(batch_premium, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-vol3-economics-retry-policies .callout-notebook title="What a retry cap buys"}

**Problem**: A cheap configuration has acceptance probability `{python} RetryBudget.p_small_str` and all-in cost `{python} RetryBudget.c_small_str` per attempt. A stronger configuration has probability `{python} RetryBudget.p_big_str` and costs `{python} RetryBudget.c_big_str`. Allow up to `{python} RetryBudget.k_str` cheap attempts under the model above. Which policy has the lowest cost per expected accepted task: sequential retry, a fully paid batch, or one stronger attempt?

**Math**: Sequential retry accepts `{python} RetryBudget.coverage_str` percent of inputs in expectation and uses `{python} RetryBudget.seq_attempts_str` attempts per input. Expected spend is `{python} RetryBudget.seq_cost_str` per input and `{python} RetryBudget.seq_per_acc_str` per accepted task. Paying for the full batch gives the same acceptance probability for `{python} RetryBudget.par_cost_str` per input and `{python} RetryBudget.par_per_acc_str` per accepted task. One stronger attempt costs `{python} RetryBudget.big_per_acc_str` per accepted task.

**Systems insight**: Under early stopping, retrying the cheap configuration beats switching to the stronger one whenever $c_{\text{small}}/p_{\text{small}} < c_{\text{big}}/p_{\text{big}}$, and here it also covers `{python} RetryBudget.coverage_str` percent of inputs against `{python} RetryBudget.p_big_pct_str`. Paying for the full batch buys the same coverage at `{python} RetryBudget.batch_premium_mult_str` the cost per accepted task, the ratio of $k$ to the expected attempt count, so a parallel batch is worth buying only for a measured deadline benefit that the objective values at more than that premium.

:::

Real tasks do not share one $p$. Hard tasks keep low acceptance across retries, so averaging per-task probabilities before applying $1-(1-p)^k$ overstates coverage and the aggregate ratio drifts from $c/p$. Measured repeated sampling shows the effect: on tasks with automatic checks, coverage, the fraction of tasks solved by any sample, keeps rising across orders of magnitude of samples, roughly log-linearly rather than saturating as a single shared $p$ would predict [@brown2024monkeys]. Feedback, outages, and shared mutable environments also break the fixed-attempt model. Retry policy is therefore priced from measured per-task retry outcomes under the evaluation protocol of @sec-vol3-evaluation.

Each additional candidate is also another chance for a false acceptance (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute), and a passing check is evidence under its declared scope, not authorization to publish. Caching, compaction, and retry policy change what the runtime purchases; the next section asks which purchased work sets the completion time.

## Critical-Path Latency {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-criticalpath}

A faster model call does not produce an equally faster repair. Tests, environment preparation, queueing, and finalization can occupy most of the elapsed interval. The economic question is how much a proposed change reduces time to a declared endpoint, what resources it consumes, and whether it preserves the required acceptance evidence. A trace locates the opportunity, and the account prices it.

### Account for dependencies and elapsed time

The tracing discipline in @sec-vol3-evaluation-tracing distinguishes an enclosing span from the work inside it. Adding a parent duration to its children's durations double-counts time. Adding concurrent children also overcounts elapsed time, while omitting queueing or uninstrumented gaps undercounts it. Preserve unexplained intervals as unexplained rather than assigning them to a convenient component.

A span's parent identifies containment, which is not always a completion dependency. Construct the execution graph from the actual dispatch and join conditions. An edge means that the later interval cannot begin before its predecessor finishes. Use nonoverlapping intervals along each path, not inclusive parents alongside their children. For a dependency graph with durations $t(v)$ and source-to-sink paths $\Pi$, its longest path, the **critical path**\index{Critical path!trajectory},[^fn-critical-path-method] is

$$T_{\text{critical}} = \max_{\pi \in \Pi} \sum_{v \in \pi} t(v).$$ {#eq-vol3-critical-path}

[^fn-critical-path-method]: **Critical Path**: The critical-path method was introduced for planning and scheduling large engineering projects, where the longest chain of dependent activities fixes the completion date and every activity off that chain has slack [@kelley1959critical]. Distributed-systems work later recovered the same dependency model from existing component logs of production requests, precisely so that critical-path and slack analysis could say which component's speedup would shorten end-to-end latency [@chow2014mystery]. An agent trace needs the same reconstruction before any acceleration is priced.

For a graph containing only required service work, @eq-vol3-critical-path is a lower bound on completion time. It represents the observed elapsed interval exactly only when the graph also accounts for actual release times, resource waits, and other delays at the chosen boundary. The observation boundary must include whatever the decision values, since a streamed answer, an assessed candidate, and a fully finalized task are different endpoints.

Shortening a nonlimiting branch leaves that endpoint unchanged under a fixed schedule, though it can release capacity or lower cost. Shortening the current longest path can make another path limiting, so the paths are recomputed after each proposed change instead of subtracting every saved component-second from the elapsed time.

### Bound the payoff of faster inference

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-critical-path
#| echo: false
# WHERE FASTER INFERENCE HELPS (LEGO)
# Goal: Bound elapsed-time savings in one fixed, serial repair episode.
# Scope: Hypothetical seconds, not measurements or a fleet workload model.
from mlsysim import second
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_qty, fmt_percent, fmt_multiple, check

class CriticalPath:
    # 1. LOAD: sequential intervals; all required work remains unchanged.
    model_intervals_s = (1.20, 8.40, 1.85, 11.20, 2.10, 4.50)
    tests_s = 245.60
    lifecycle_intervals_s = (14.80, 22.55)
    runtime_status_intervals_s = (0.12, 0.08)
    model_speedup = 4.0

    # 2. EXECUTE: each interval belongs to exactly one category.
    model_s = sum(model_intervals_s)
    lifecycle_s = sum(lifecycle_intervals_s)
    runtime_status_s = sum(runtime_status_intervals_s)
    other_s = tests_s + lifecycle_s + runtime_status_s
    total_s = model_s + other_s
    model_fraction = model_s / total_s
    changed_s = other_s + model_s / model_speedup
    saving_s = total_s - changed_s
    speedup = total_s / changed_s
    limiting_speedup = total_s / other_s
    tests_half_saving_s = tests_s / 2  # alternative: halve the required test interval

    # 3. GUARD: disjoint accounting and independent Amdahl calculation.
    check(all(t >= 0 for t in model_intervals_s + lifecycle_intervals_s + runtime_status_intervals_s), "Nonnegative intervals")
    check(tests_s >= 0 and other_s > 0 and model_speedup >= 1, "Valid acceleration domain")
    check(abs(total_s - 312.40) < 1e-9, "Full declared elapsed interval")
    check(abs(changed_s - total_s * (1 - model_fraction + model_fraction / model_speedup)) < 1e-9, "Independent Amdahl calculation")
    check(abs(saving_s - 21.9375) < 1e-9, "Independent saved model time")
    check(1 <= speedup <= limiting_speedup, "Finite acceleration respects limiting bound")
    check(tests_half_saving_s > 5 * saving_s, "Halving tests must dominate the model speedup here")

    # 4. OUTPUT: each export is used below, with units supplied once.
    model_str = fmt_qty(model_s * second, second, precision=2)
    tests_str = fmt_qty(tests_s * second, second, precision=2)
    lifecycle_str = fmt_qty(lifecycle_s * second, second, precision=2)
    runtime_status_str = fmt_qty(runtime_status_s * second, second, precision=2)
    total_str = fmt_qty(total_s * second, second, precision=2)
    fraction_str = fmt_percent(model_fraction, precision=1, style="prose")
    model_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(model_speedup, precision=0)
    changed_str = fmt_qty(changed_s * second, second, precision=2)
    saving_str = fmt_qty(saving_s * second, second, precision=2)
    speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(speedup, precision=2)
    limiting_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(limiting_speedup, precision=2)
    tests_half_saving_str = fmt_qty(tests_half_saving_s * second, second, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-18-critical-path-investment .callout-notebook title="How much does faster inference buy?"}

**Problem**: In a hypothetical three-turn repair episode, how much elapsed time does a `{python} CriticalPath.model_speedup_mult_str` acceleration of every model call save?

**Variables**: All intervals run sequentially, from runtime initialization through the required sandbox snapshot export, with no queueing, overlap, or unaccounted gap. The grouped durations in @tbl-vol3-trace-critical-path are disjoint sums, not nested spans or a chronological listing. The acceleration changes no output, tool work, evidence coverage, scheduling, or finalization.

| Disjoint category                            |                               Elapsed time |
|:---------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------:|
| Model calls across the three turns           |          `{python} CriticalPath.model_str` |
| Required test execution                      |          `{python} CriticalPath.tests_str` |
| Sandbox creation and snapshot export         |      `{python} CriticalPath.lifecycle_str` |
| Runtime initialization and repository status | `{python} CriticalPath.runtime_status_str` |
| **Whole declared interval**                  |      **`{python} CriticalPath.total_str`** |

: **One serial repair episode**: Categories partition elapsed time under the stated assumptions; the total is not an additional interval. {#tbl-vol3-trace-critical-path}

**Math**: If model work occupies fraction $f$ of the original time $T$ and becomes $x$ times faster, with $x \geq 1$, then $T' = T[(1-f)+f/x]$, Amdahl's fixed-work bound [@amdahl1967]. Here model work occupies `{python} CriticalPath.fraction_str`. A `{python} CriticalPath.model_speedup_mult_str` model acceleration gives a projected `{python} CriticalPath.changed_str` episode, saving `{python} CriticalPath.saving_str` and yielding a whole-episode speedup of `{python} CriticalPath.speedup_mult_str`. Even instantaneous model work would give only `{python} CriticalPath.limiting_speedup_mult_str` under these assumptions.

**Systems insight**: The ceiling $1/(1-f)$ decides whether model speed is worth buying, and it can be computed before any purchase. Halving the test interval at the same coverage would save `{python} CriticalPath.tests_half_saving_str`, several times the model speedup's `{python} CriticalPath.saving_str`, and it would also shorten the sandbox holding charge in $C_{\text{eff}}$. When the deadline gap exceeds what $1/(1-f)$ allows, the investment belongs on tests and sandbox lifecycle; in a branching trajectory the same test applies to the recomputed critical path of @eq-vol3-critical-path.

:::

### Shorten the path without weakening the result

Once the trace names the limiting path, each kind of span on it has its own cause and its own lever. @Tbl-vol3-span-taxonomy maps the span types of @sec-vol3-evaluation-tracing to what sets their duration and what shortens them.

| Span                 | What sets its duration                         | What shortens it                                                         |
|:---------------------|:-----------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Model, reading input | Context length, prefix-cache misses, queueing  | Cache-stable layout, smaller context, less queueing                      |
| Model, generating    | Output and reasoning tokens                    | Shorter outputs, smaller reasoning budget, speculative decoding          |
| Sandbox and tools    | Build size, test-suite size, cold starts       | Warm pools, snapshots, build caches, test selection, parallel tool calls |
| Network and services | Round trips, payload size, provider throttling | Response caching, prefetching, rate-limit headroom                       |
| Runtime              | Parsing, validation, logging, snapshotting     | Streaming parsers, incremental snapshots                                 |

: **Trajectory Span Types**: What bounds each kind of span on an agent's critical path and which techniques shorten it. Each lever is admissible only if the accepted result still meets the same acceptance contract and coverage. {#tbl-vol3-span-taxonomy}

Independent tool calls can overlap when their dependencies, authority, and resource reservations permit it. If they start together, do not interfere, and all must finish before continuation, the join waits for the longest call rather than their sum; contention, staggered starts, or one call consuming another's output bring back part of the sum. Cached builds and warm environments shorten the sandbox span under the isolation and reset conditions of @sec-vol3-sandboxes.

Preparation can overlap model generation when it runs under its own scope and resource admission and performs no proposed effect before the complete call is validated and authorized. A partially streamed call is not an authorized request, and even a file read can cross an access boundary. Discarded preparation stays in the account, and its resources are released.

Early stopping changes the observation as well as its duration. A failed mandatory test establishes that the candidate fails that criterion; an early pass says nothing about the rest of the suite. Test selection and streaming failures therefore accelerate diagnosis, while final acceptance still runs its declared coverage, and a canceled check stays in the account until its work settles (@sec-vol3-failure-recovery).

### Profitability boundaries for speculative decoding {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-speculative}

@Sec-vol3-foundation-model introduced speculative decoding as a serving technique whose output and performance depend on its implementation and sampling assumptions. Here it is an economic option, worth buying only if it improves the task-level objective enough to justify its resource cost.

A small draft model[^fn-speculative-draft-lineage] proposes $\gamma$ tokens per round, and the target model checks them in one pass, keeping the prefix it accepts and emitting one token of its own [@leviathan2023fast; @chen2023accelerating]. Let a draft token cost a fraction $\beta$ of one target decoding step, and let $\bar m$ be the mean number of draft tokens accepted per round. If verifying a round costs about one target step, each round emits $\bar m+1$ tokens in the time of $\gamma\beta+1$ target steps, so the decoding speedup for one stream is

$$S_{\text{spec}}=\frac{\bar m+1}{\gamma\beta+1}.$$ {#eq-vol3-spec-speedup}

[^fn-speculative-draft-lineage]: **Draft-then-Verify Decoding**: The idea predates large language models. Blockwise parallel decoding predicted several future positions at once and backed off to the longest prefix a scoring model validated [@stern2018blockwise]. Speculative decoding moved the proposals into a separate small draft model and added an acceptance rule under which sampled outputs keep the target model's distribution, which is why its savings are purely a cost and latency question rather than a quality trade.

Speculation shortens the call only when $\bar m>\gamma\beta$, that is, when accepted drafts repay the draft work; below that boundary it slows the stream it was meant to accelerate. The one-step verification assumption holds when single-stream decoding is limited by reading model state rather than by arithmetic (principle \ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}), and it weakens as batching makes the target's arithmetic busy.

The boundary prices decoding steps within one call. The complete serving path adds draft generation, coordination, setup, and work discarded at rejection or early stopping, which short and interrupted responses pay with little return. Under load, the draft model also occupies memory and compute that could serve another request, and verification changes the target's scheduling. The policy is therefore measured under the intended load, comparing complete-call latency, total resource use, queueing, and downstream task acceptance against the same baseline workload; a high draft-token acceptance rate is a call-level measurement, not task acceptance.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-spec-composition
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SPECULATIVE SPEEDUP COMPOSED WITH THE TRAJECTORY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @eq-vol3-spec-speedup in @sec-vol3-agent-economics-speculative.
# │ Goal: Show the call-level boundary and its bounded trajectory payoff.
# │ Show: Speedup above and below break-even; effect on the serial episode.
# │ How:  S = (m + 1) / (gamma * r + 1), then T' = T[(1 - f) + f / S].
# │ Note: Reads CriticalPath (model share, episode length) from the earlier
# │       cell. Draft length, cost ratio, and acceptance are scenario inputs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_qty

class SpecComposition:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario inputs; episode from CriticalPath) ──────────────
    gamma = 5  # scenario: draft tokens proposed per round
    r = 0.08  # scenario: draft token cost as a fraction of a target step
    m_high, m_low = 3.6, 0.3  # scenario: mean accepted draft tokens per round
    f = CriticalPath.model_fraction
    total_s = CriticalPath.total_s

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Call-level speedup, then fixed-work composition) ─────
    breakeven = gamma * r
    s_high = (m_high + 1) / (gamma * r + 1)
    s_low = (m_low + 1) / (gamma * r + 1)
    t_high = total_s * ((1 - f) + f / s_high)
    t_low = total_s * ((1 - f) + f / s_low)
    traj_high = total_s / t_high
    traj_bound = 1 / (1 - f)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(m_high > breakeven > m_low >= 0, "One case on each side of the break-even")
    check(s_high > 1 > s_low, "Break-even separates speedup from slowdown")
    check(1 < traj_high < traj_bound and t_low > total_s, "Trajectory gain is bounded; slowdown lengthens it")
    check(abs(traj_bound - CriticalPath.limiting_speedup) < 1e-9, "Same bound as the instant-model case")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    gamma_str = fmt_int(gamma)
    r_str = fmt(r, precision=2)
    breakeven_str = fmt(breakeven, precision=1)
    m_high_str, m_low_str = fmt(m_high, precision=1), fmt(m_low, precision=1)
    s_high_mult_str = fmt_multiple(s_high, precision=2)
    s_low_mult_str = fmt_multiple(s_low, precision=2)
    t_high_str = fmt_qty(t_high * second, second, precision=1)
    t_low_str = fmt_qty(t_low * second, second, precision=1)
    traj_high_mult_str = fmt_multiple(traj_high, precision=2)
```

A measured call-level speedup is carried back to the trajectory with the fixed-work argument of notebook \ref{nbk-18-critical-path-investment}, substituting $S_{\text{spec}}$ for $x$, so the trajectory gains at most $1/(1-f)$.

Suppose each round drafts `{python} SpecComposition.gamma_str` tokens, each costing `{python} SpecComposition.r_str` of a target step, so the break-even is `{python} SpecComposition.breakeven_str` accepted tokens per round. Accepting `{python} SpecComposition.m_high_str` per round gives `{python} SpecComposition.s_high_mult_str` on the call by @eq-vol3-spec-speedup. Even granting that speedup to every model interval of the serial episode in @tbl-vol3-trace-critical-path, the episode shrinks from `{python} CriticalPath.total_str` to `{python} SpecComposition.t_high_str`, a `{python} SpecComposition.traj_high_mult_str` whole-episode speedup. A workload that accepts only `{python} SpecComposition.m_low_str` per round falls below the boundary, runs its calls at `{python} SpecComposition.s_low_mult_str`, and lengthens the episode to `{python} SpecComposition.t_low_str`. @Fig-vol3-critical-path-waterfall draws these interventions against the same episode.

::: {#fig-vol3-critical-path-waterfall fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Faster Model Calls, a Barely Shorter Episode**: The serial repair episode of @tbl-vol3-trace-critical-path drawn to scale, each bar partitioned into disjoint category sums rather than a chronological trace. Required tests and sandbox lifecycle form a non-model floor that no model acceleration crosses. A `{python} CriticalPath.model_speedup_mult_str` model speedup and a `{python} SpecComposition.s_high_mult_str` speculative speedup on the calls each shorten the episode by less than a tenth, and even instant model calls stop at the floor. The runtime-status interval is too short to draw at this scale." fig-alt="Four horizontal stacked bars on a shared elapsed-time axis. Each bar has a long required-tests segment, a shorter sandbox creation and export segment, and a model-calls segment at its right end, with its end time and speedup labeled. The model segment is widest in the baseline bar, narrower for model calls four times faster and for speculative decoding, and absent for instant model calls. A dashed red line marks the non-model floor where the model segment begins, and a dashed gray line marks the baseline end."}
![](images/svg/fig-vol3-critical-path-waterfall.svg)
:::

An acceleration on a limiting path may buy deadline headroom; one elsewhere may primarily buy capacity or cost savings. A policy can be worth purchasing despite higher expense when the time benefit is valuable, or worth rejecting despite faster token generation when contention erases that benefit. The rule therefore has two boundaries: speculation must clear $\bar m>\gamma\beta$ on the call under the intended load, and the trajectory can gain at most $1/(1-f)$ from it.

- [ ] **Cache layout**: Which term of @eq-vol3-agent-economics-session-bill grows when a timestamp moves from the end of the system prompt to its front, and how does that term's growth with the horizon change?
- [ ] **Compaction payback**: With `{python} PrefixCacheCost.before_str` calls left in notebook \ref{nbk-vol3-compaction-crossing}, should the runtime compact for price alone? What else could justify compacting anyway?

## Model Cascades and Routing {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-cascades}

Critical-path analysis identifies where faster execution matters; routing decides which configuration should attempt the work at all. A specialized model may complete a constrained transformation inexpensively, while another configuration may be worth its higher cost for diagnosis. A **model cascade**\index{Model cascade!definition}[^fn-cascade-viola-jones] tries one configuration and conditionally escalates to another, an approach explored for language model APIs in FrugalGPT [@chen2023frugalgpt]. Its economic value depends on what the lower tiers resolve, what their failures cost, and which tasks remain for later tiers.

[^fn-cascade-viola-jones]: **Classifier Cascade**: The design pattern is older than language models. A real-time face detector chained increasingly expensive classifiers so that cheap early stages discarded most background regions and the costly stages ran only on the promising remainder [@viola2001]. Its speed came from the early exit rate, which is the same quantity that sets a model cascade's cost here.

Every exit must satisfy the same declared acceptance contract. A schema check suffices for a purely syntactic transformation and cannot establish that a source patch preserves authentication behavior; the tier's price neither strengthens nor weakens the contract. Publication and effect authorization remain separate runtime decisions.

### Direct routing and conditional escalation

A **direct router**\index{Direct router!definition} selects a configuration before generation, from available task features. A cascade instead buys an initial attempt and uses its assessment to decide whether to continue, so the two policies need different accounts. A mistaken direct route lowers acceptance or misses a deadline; a mistaken cheap-first choice spends budget and time before escalating, even when a later tier resolves the task.

For a three-tier cascade, let $q_j$ be the probability of acceptance at tier $j$, conditional on reaching it. Assume every task not accepted at a lower tier continues to the next tier, with no additional retry, cancellation, or stopping branch. The **reach probabilities**\index{Reach probability!definition}, the chance that a task arrives at each tier, are $r_1=1$, $r_2=1-q_1$, and $r_3=(1-q_1)(1-q_2)$. The product is the probability chain rule, not an assumption that tiers fail independently. Later tiers receive the selected remainder, so their conditional acceptance rates cannot be copied from a full-workload benchmark.

Let $c_j$ be mean generation and associated execution cost conditional on reaching tier $j$, excluding its gate, and let $g_j$ be that gate's mean cost. Let $t_j$ and $v_j$ be the corresponding mean durations. Count preparation, assessment, and cleanup in the appropriate terms rather than pricing only output tokens. Linearity of expectation gives

$$
\mathbb{E}[C_{\mathrm{cascade}}]=\sum_{j=1}^{3}r_j(c_j+g_j),
\qquad p_{\mathrm{acc}}=\sum_{j=1}^{3}r_jq_j.
$$

For a serial cascade with all elapsed intervals represented, its mean duration is

$$
\mathbb{E}[T_{\mathrm{cascade}}]=\sum_{j=1}^{3}r_j(t_j+v_j).
$$

The final tier pays for its gate too. With fixed durations, a task reaching every tier takes $\sum_j(t_j+v_j)$; with variable durations and queueing, tail percentiles need the measured distribution. A policy that stops early or leaves assessments unresolved uses its actual reach probabilities and reports those outcomes separately.

The planning form of cost per accepted task is $\mathbb{E}[C_{\mathrm{cascade}}]/p_{\mathrm{acc}}$, which charges every reached tier rather than only the successful paths. A direct frontier policy needs its own acceptance rate on the full target cohort, since its rate on the harder escalated subset is a different quantity.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-cascade
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COST AND ACCEPTANCE OF A THREE-TIER CASCADE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The routing comparison under one unchanged acceptance contract.
# │ Goal: Price every reached tier, including its final assessment.
# │ Show: Resolved counts, cost per accepted task, and fixed-scenario durations.
# │ How: Reconcile a hypothetical completed cohort with conditional reach sums.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import ureg
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_time, fmt_usd

class CascadeCost:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    tasks = 100_000  # hypothetical completed cohort per policy
    calls = (0.0004, 0.0020, 0.0600)  # dollars per reached tier, gate excluded
    gate_cost = 0.0010  # dollars per assessment, same contract at every tier
    call_seconds = (0.25, 0.80, 4.50)
    gate_seconds = 0.40
    accepted_by_tier = (60_000, 28_000, 11_400)
    direct_accepted = 97_000  # separate stipulated full-cohort baseline

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    reached = (tasks, tasks - accepted_by_tier[0], tasks - accepted_by_tier[0] - accepted_by_tier[1])
    spend, elapsed_sum = 0.0, 0.0
    conditional, reaches = [], []
    for j in range(3):
        conditional.append(accepted_by_tier[j] / reached[j])
        reaches.append(reached[j] / tasks)
        spend += reached[j] * (calls[j] + gate_cost)
        elapsed_sum += reached[j] * (call_seconds[j] + gate_seconds)
    accepted = sum(accepted_by_tier)
    unresolved = tasks - accepted
    per_initiated = spend / tasks
    per_accepted = spend / accepted
    direct_spend = tasks * (calls[-1] + gate_cost)
    direct_per_accepted = direct_spend / direct_accepted
    mean_seconds = elapsed_sum / tasks
    all_tiers_seconds = sum(call_seconds) + 3 * gate_seconds
    direct_seconds = call_seconds[-1] + gate_seconds
    direct_ratio = direct_per_accepted / per_accepted
    lower_tier_toll = calls[0] + calls[1] + 2 * gate_cost  # paid by every task reaching tier 3

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(tasks > 0 and 0 < direct_accepted <= tasks, "baseline denominator")
    check(all(0 <= q <= 1 for q in conditional), "conditional acceptance")
    check(accepted + unresolved == tasks and accepted > 0, "cohort conservation")
    check(math.isclose(reaches[2], (1 - conditional[0]) * (1 - conditional[1])), "conditional reach chain")
    expected_cost = 0.0
    for r, c in zip(reaches, calls):
        expected_cost += r * (c + gate_cost)
    check(math.isclose(per_initiated, expected_cost), "cost ledger matches expectation")
    check(per_accepted < direct_per_accepted, "stipulated cost comparison")
    check(all_tiers_seconds > direct_seconds and lower_tier_toll < calls[-1], "escalation costs time more than money")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    tasks_str = fmt_int(tasks)
    call_costs_str = ", ".join(fmt_usd(c, precision=4) for c in calls)
    call_times_str = ", ".join(fmt_time(t, ureg.second, precision=2) for t in call_seconds)
    gate_cost_str = fmt_usd(gate_cost, precision=4)
    gate_time_str = fmt_time(gate_seconds, ureg.second, precision=2)
    first_accepted_str = fmt_int(accepted_by_tier[0])
    second_accepted_str = fmt_int(accepted_by_tier[1])
    third_accepted_str = fmt_int(accepted_by_tier[2])
    second_reached_str = fmt_int(reached[1])
    third_reached_str = fmt_int(reached[2])
    conditional_rates_str = ", ".join(fmt_percent(q, precision=0, style="prose") for q in conditional)
    direct_accepted_str = fmt_int(direct_accepted)
    accepted_str = fmt_int(accepted)
    unresolved_str = fmt_int(unresolved)
    acceptance_str = fmt_percent(accepted / tasks, precision=1, style="prose")
    spend_str = fmt_usd(spend, precision=0)
    per_initiated_str = fmt_usd(per_initiated, precision=5)
    per_accepted_str = fmt_usd(per_accepted, precision=5)
    direct_spend_str = fmt_usd(direct_spend, precision=0)
    direct_per_accepted_str = fmt_usd(direct_per_accepted, precision=5)
    mean_time_str = fmt_time(mean_seconds, ureg.second, precision=3)
    all_tiers_time_str = fmt_time(all_tiers_seconds, ureg.second, precision=2)
    direct_time_str = fmt_time(direct_seconds, ureg.second, precision=2)
    direct_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(direct_ratio, precision=1)
    first_exit_str = fmt_percent(accepted_by_tier[0] / tasks, precision=0, style="prose")
    lower_tier_toll_str = fmt_usd(lower_tier_toll, precision=4)
```

::: {#nbk-18-cost-and-latency-trade-offs-in .callout-notebook title="Price the accepted result at every exit"}

**Problem:** For hypothetical cohorts of `{python} CascadeCost.tasks_str` small source-editing tasks per policy, should a team choose the cascade or direct frontier execution to minimize cost per accepted result, and what duration trade-off accompanies that choice?

**Variables:** Every candidate faces the same scoped acceptance procedure. In tier order, the cascade's generation and execution charges, excluding assessment, are `{python} CascadeCost.call_costs_str` per reached tier, with fixed durations of `{python} CascadeCost.call_times_str`. Each assessment costs `{python} CascadeCost.gate_cost_str` and takes `{python} CascadeCost.gate_time_str`, including the final one. These stipulated charges include all execution, cleanup, and allocated shared overhead within the example's boundary; there is no queue wait or human completion, and all bills and assessments are settled at the cutoff.

The cascade accepts `{python} CascadeCost.first_accepted_str` tasks at tier 1, `{python} CascadeCost.second_accepted_str` of the `{python} CascadeCost.second_reached_str` reaching tier 2, and `{python} CascadeCost.third_accepted_str` of the `{python} CascadeCost.third_reached_str` reaching tier 3. The conditional acceptance rates are therefore `{python} CascadeCost.conditional_rates_str`, respectively. For comparison, a separate direct-to-frontier policy is stipulated to accept `{python} CascadeCost.direct_accepted_str` of its equally sized full cohort. That full-cohort rate is an independent scenario input, not inferred from the cascade's selected remainder.

**Math:** The cascade accepts `{python} CascadeCost.accepted_str` tasks, or `{python} CascadeCost.acceptance_str`, and leaves `{python} CascadeCost.unresolved_str` unaccepted. It spends `{python} CascadeCost.spend_str` in total: `{python} CascadeCost.per_initiated_str` per initiated task and `{python} CascadeCost.per_accepted_str` per accepted result. Direct frontier execution spends `{python} CascadeCost.direct_spend_str`, or `{python} CascadeCost.direct_per_accepted_str` per accepted result. The lower-tier attempts are paid for whether or not they pass.

Under the fixed-duration assumptions, the cascade takes `{python} CascadeCost.mean_time_str` on average, while its all-tier path takes `{python} CascadeCost.all_tiers_time_str`. Direct execution takes `{python} CascadeCost.direct_time_str`, including assessment.

**Systems insight**: Direct execution costs `{python} CascadeCost.direct_ratio_mult_str` as much per accepted result as the cascade, because `{python} CascadeCost.first_exit_str` of tasks exit at a tier whose call and gate cost a small fraction of the frontier call. Its price is time, not money: each escalated task pays only `{python} CascadeCost.lower_tier_toll_str` in lower-tier tolls but waits `{python} CascadeCost.all_tiers_time_str` instead of `{python} CascadeCost.direct_time_str`. The saving scales with the first tier's exit rate, so the lever is the router: sending tasks predicted to escalate straight to the frontier tier removes the time penalty where a deadline binds while keeping the cost advantage elsewhere.

:::

@Fig-vol3-model-cascade-flowchart traces that cohort through the tiers. Every reached tier pays for its call and its gate, and only the remainder that a gate rejects reaches the next tier.

::: {#fig-vol3-model-cascade-flowchart fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**A Gated Three-Tier Cascade**: Every tier's candidate faces the same acceptance contract, and every gate charges its assessment whether or not the candidate passes, including the final gate. Accepted results exit at the tier that produced them and only the rejected remainder escalates, so reach falls from `{python} CascadeCost.tasks_str` tasks to `{python} CascadeCost.third_reached_str`. The ledger compares cost per accepted result, which charges every rejected attempt to the accepted outcomes, with the separately stipulated direct frontier baseline." fig-alt="Flow diagram. An initiated-tasks box feeds tier 1 and then a gate labeled same contract. Pass arrows lead from each gate to an accepted box, and reject arrows lead down from the tier 1 and tier 2 gates to the next tier, each followed by its own gate. The tier 3 gate's reject arrow ends in an unresolved box, and a total accepted box sits below the accepted column. Two ledger boxes at the bottom give the cascade's total cost, cost per initiated task, and cost per accepted result, and the direct frontier policy's total cost, accepted count, and cost per accepted result."}
![](images/svg/multi_agent_token_cascade_routing_v2.svg)
:::

### Gate errors and the decision to continue

The cost ledger counts gate decisions even when a gate is wrong. An observed accepted result is not automatically a correct result under every intended property. To price an additional consequence, define $\mathrm{FA}$ as the event that an initiated task is accepted yet violates an independently assessed criterion, and define $C_{\mathrm{harm}}$ as its additional harm or remediation cost not already included in the execution ledger. The expected cost per initiated task including this term is

$$
\mathbb{E}[C_{\mathrm{with\ harm}}]
=\mathbb{E}[C_{\mathrm{cascade}}]+P(\mathrm{FA})\,\mathbb{E}[C_{\mathrm{harm}}\mid \mathrm{FA}].
$$

The harm term sits beside cost per accepted task rather than redefining it, and its probability is taken over initiated tasks. A false-accept fraction measured among accepted results is multiplied by the acceptance probability to give $P(\mathrm{FA})$, and a false acceptance rate measured among invalid candidates (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute) has a different denominator again. Irreparable consequences stay under authority and risk limits whatever their expected value.

Escalation passes the next tier bounded diagnostic evidence and the failed candidate's identity, treated as untrusted, rather than the whole failed transcript, and it keeps pending or unavailable assessments distinct from definite rejection. A passing assessment yields an accepted-candidate record; publication still checks current dependencies, authority, and any required operation-bound approval.

A learned router can estimate the probability and cost of each eligible remaining policy from evaluation data, for example by training on preference comparisons between a stronger and a weaker model [@ong2024routellm]. Its training records must reflect which configurations were actually tried; logs from a selective router do not reveal every untried configuration's counterfactual result.[^fn-counterfactual-router-logs]

[^fn-counterfactual-router-logs]: **Counterfactual Logs**: Learning from the logs of a deployed selection policy is a causal-inference problem, worked out at scale for online ad placement, where the system only observes outcomes of the choices it made [@bottou2013counterfactual]. Estimating what another policy would have achieved requires that the logging policy explored with known probabilities, so a router that never sends an easy-looking task to the frontier tier leaves no evidence about what that route would have bought. For a simple monetary objective, suppose policies $X$ and $Y$ offer acceptance probabilities $p_X,p_Y$ and expected additional costs $C_X,C_Y$ conditional on the current task information. If the same accepted outcome is valued at $V$, rejected outcomes have zero value, and other consequences are equal or already counted, prefer $Y$ when

$$
V(p_Y-p_X)>C_Y-C_X.
$$

For direct routing, the rule compares two complete direct policies. After a failed cheap attempt, it compares the remaining escalation policy with stopping or another eligible action, and already incurred spend is sunk. A cheap-then-frontier policy has its own reach-weighted cost and acceptance probability, not merely the cheap model's price. The rule operates inside the remaining budget, deadline, and authority limits; economic value never licenses spending past a limit or substitutes for authorization.

Load changes the comparison. Waiting for a tier consumes elapsed time and can retain a sandbox, so a route with a higher call price can win when the cheap tier's queue is long, and current queue information belongs in the estimates of remaining cost and completion time.
