The next section supplies the capacity model for those waits.

## Capacity for Trajectories {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-capacity}

A routing policy changes the work arriving at each model and tool service. Capacity planning asks whether those services can sustain that work within the task's latency and resource constraints. The unit entering the platform is a trajectory; the units entering its bottlenecks are model calls, tool operations, and resource leases. Their arrival rates and residence times are different.

### Residence, service, and quota

For a stable population with finite long-run averages, Little's law [@little1961] (@sec-vol3-kv-workload-dynamics) relates the mean number of admitted trajectories present, $N_{\text{traj}}$, to their admission rate $\lambda_{\text{traj}}$ and mean time from admission to departure, $\mathbb{E}[T_{\text{traj}}]$:

$$N_{\text{traj}} = \lambda_{\text{traj}}\mathbb{E}[T_{\text{traj}}].$$ {#eq-vol3-trajectory-concurrency}

The population and boundary must match. Rejected arrivals stay outside this population, while admitted attempts that eventually fail count. A trajectory waiting for approval is present without occupying a model worker, so the same law is applied separately to sandbox leases, retained attention state, active model service, and unsettled operations, each with its own holding interval. @Sec-vol3-appendix-inference-queueing works a tool-wait example that separates live-trajectory counts from attention-state occupancy under different retention policies.

Little's law gives a mean; peak concurrency and the reserve a latency percentile needs come from the holding policy and the observed occupancy distribution. Call demand follows the number of calls per admitted attempt, including retries and delegated calls within the boundary, with mean rate $\lambda_{\text{call}}=\lambda_{\text{traj}}\mathbb{E}[N_{\text{call}}]$ under stable flow. Those arrivals can be correlated: a cohort reaching the same tool boundary arrives as a burst.

Acceptance couples this demand to the cost account. To deliver accepted tasks at rate $\lambda_{\text{acc}}$ when a fraction $\alpha$ of admitted attempts is accepted, the platform must admit

$$\lambda_{\text{traj}}=\frac{\lambda_{\text{acc}}}{\alpha},
\qquad
\rho(\alpha)=\frac{\lambda_{\text{acc}}\,\mathbb{E}[N_{\text{call}}]}{\alpha\,N_{\mathrm{w}}\mu}$$

for a pool of $N_{\mathrm{w}}$ model workers, each completing $\mu$ calls per unit time. The accepted rate $\lambda_{\text{acc}}$ is the quantity the platform exists to deliver.

::: {#dfn-18-trajectory-goodput .callout-definition title="Trajectory goodput"}

***Trajectory goodput***\index{Trajectory goodput!definition} is the number of distinct tasks accepted under a declared contract per unit of elapsed observation time.

1. **Significance**: It is the throughput a trajectory platform is sized for. At acceptance fraction $\alpha$, every unit of goodput requires $1/\alpha$ admitted trajectories, so acceptance sets both the spending multiplier in $C_{\text{eff}}$ and the offered load $\rho(\alpha)$.
2. **Distinction**: Token, call, and trajectory throughput count work performed; goodput counts only accepted outcomes. Goodput per dollar divides the same accepted count by total cost instead of elapsed time.
3. **Common pitfall**: Counting repeated accepted attempts at one task, or completions outside the declared contract, as additional goodput.

:::

The next calculation sizes one hypothetical fleet from its admission rate and asks which resource binds first.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-trajectory-capacity
#| echo: false
from mlsysim import *

class TrajectoryCapacity:
    # 1. LOAD: hypothetical stationary admitted population; token counts
    # include all input/output tokens charged against this scenario's quota.
    arrival = 1 / minute
    residence = 20 * minute
    calls = 60
    tokens_per_call = 30_000
    quota = 2_000_000 / minute

    # 2. EXECUTE: mean resource demand, not burst or deadline feasibility.
    concurrent = (arrival * residence).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    call_rate = arrival * calls
    tokens_per_trajectory = calls * tokens_per_call
    demand = arrival * tokens_per_trajectory
    quota_share = (demand / quota).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    arrival_ceiling = quota / tokens_per_trajectory
    # At fixed goodput, admissions scale as 1/alpha; this relative drop in
    # acceptance raises admissions to the quota ceiling.
    acceptance_margin = 1 - quota_share

    # 3. GUARD
    check(arrival > 0 / minute and residence > 0 * second, "Positive flow and residence")
    check(calls > 0 and tokens_per_call > 0 and quota > 0 / minute, "Positive demand inputs")
    check(0 < quota_share < 1, "This scenario fits the mean token quota only")

    # 4. OUTPUT
    arrival_str = fmt((arrival * minute).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude, precision=0)
    residence_str = fmt_time(residence, minute, precision=0, style="word")
    calls_str = fmt_int(calls)
    tokens_per_call_str = fmt_int(tokens_per_call)
    quota_str = fmt_int((quota * minute).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude)
    concurrent_str = fmt(concurrent, precision=0)
    call_rate_str = fmt_int((call_rate * minute).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude)
    tokens_per_trajectory_str = fmt_int(tokens_per_trajectory)
    demand_str = fmt_int((demand * minute).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude)
    quota_share_str = fmt_percent(quota_share, precision=0, style="prose")
    arrival_ceiling_str = fmt((arrival_ceiling * minute).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude, precision=2)
    acceptance_margin_str = fmt_percent(acceptance_margin, precision=0, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-18-trajectory-residence-and-quota .callout-notebook title="One arrival rate, different resource demands"}

**Problem**: A hypothetical fleet has a trajectory admission rate of `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.arrival_str` per minute; an attempt remains present for `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.residence_str` on average. It makes `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.calls_str` calls on average, each consuming `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.tokens_per_call_str` quota-accounted tokens on average across calls. In this scenario the provider counts input and output tokens, including cached input, toward a shared token-rate allowance of `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.quota_str` tokens per minute. What mean concurrency and token demand does this imply?

**Math**: Apply @eq-vol3-trajectory-concurrency to admitted attempts, and multiply the long-run call rate by mean tokens per call. The token average is call-weighted, not the unweighted mean of per-task averages.

**Result**: Mean trajectory concurrency is `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.concurrent_str`, while the mean call arrival rate is `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.call_rate_str` calls per minute. The mean token demand is `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.tokens_per_trajectory_str` per trajectory, giving a token rate of `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.demand_str` tokens per minute and using `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.quota_share_str` of the allowance. The quota alone permits a trajectory admission rate of at most `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.arrival_ceiling_str` per minute at this workload mix in the long run.

**Systems insight**: The token quota, not concurrency, is the binding limit, and acceptance moves it. Holding goodput fixed, admissions scale as $1/\alpha$, so a relative drop in acceptance of `{python} TrajectoryCapacity.acceptance_margin_str` would push mean demand to the full allowance with no headroom left for bursts. A model or prompt change that lowers acceptance is therefore also a capacity change. Burst fit, deadline feasibility, and sandbox residency need the quota's actual window semantics and workload traces on top of these means.

:::

Provider limits can count requests, tokens, concurrent calls, or other units over different scopes and windows, and admission follows the actual contract; a billing discount for cached input leaves the quota where it was. Reserving capacity for already admitted work can be a useful policy, decided by remaining resource needs, deadlines, fairness, and expected task value; money already spent is sunk and is no reason on its own to prioritize a task.

### The price of queueing

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-queue-price
#| echo: false
from mlsysim import *

class QueuePrice:
    # 1. LOAD: illustrative single-server model just specified in the text.
    service = 1 * second
    ca2, cs2 = 2.0, 4.0
    rho_low, rho_high = 0.70, 0.90
    holding_dollars_per_second = 0.002

    # 2. EXECUTE
    variability = (ca2 + cs2) / 2
    wait_low = variability * rho_low / (1 - rho_low) * service
    wait_high = variability * rho_high / (1 - rho_high) * service
    holding_low = wait_low.to(second).magnitude * holding_dollars_per_second
    holding_high = wait_high.to(second).magnitude * holding_dollars_per_second
    wait_ratio = (wait_high / wait_low).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    throughput_gain = rho_high / rho_low - 1

    # 3. GUARD
    check(service > 0 * second and ca2 >= 0 and cs2 >= 0, "Valid mean and variability")
    check(0 < rho_low < rho_high < 1, "Both modeled queues are stable")
    check(holding_dollars_per_second >= 0 and wait_high > wait_low, "Nonnegative holding cost")
    check(wait_ratio > 1 + 5 * throughput_gain, "Wait grows much faster than throughput near saturation")

    # 4. OUTPUT
    service_str = fmt_time(service, second, precision=0, style="word")
    ca2_str = fmt(ca2, precision=0)
    cs2_str = fmt(cs2, precision=0)
    rho_low_str = fmt_percent(rho_low, precision=0, style="prose")
    rho_high_str = fmt_percent(rho_high, precision=0, style="prose")
    wait_low_str = fmt_time(wait_low, second, precision=0, style="word")
    wait_high_str = fmt_time(wait_high, second, precision=0, style="word")
    holding_rate_str = fmt_usd(holding_dollars_per_second, precision=3)
    holding_low_str = fmt_usd(holding_low, precision=3)
    holding_high_str = fmt_usd(holding_high, precision=3)
    wait_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(wait_ratio, precision=1)
    throughput_gain_str = fmt_percent(throughput_gain, precision=1, style="prose")
```

The repair agent's model calls share a serving pool with every other trajectory on the platform. The pool runs at `{python} QueuePrice.rho_low_str` utilization, and a proposal to push it to `{python} QueuePrice.rho_high_str` would lower its price per call. The extra throughput appears on the bill. The extra waiting does not, because it lands as elapsed time on every serial call of every trajectory while sandboxes and attention state stay held.

The smallest model that prices this trade is one nonpreemptive, first-come-first-served server fed by a stationary renewal stream. Interarrival times are independent and identically distributed with mean $1/\lambda_{\text{call}}$; service times $T_s$ are independent and identically distributed; the two sequences are independent, with finite variances; and there is no batching, priority, abandonment, or feedback. Write $c_a^2$ and $c_s^2$ for the squared coefficients of variation[^fn-scv-arrival-burstiness] (variance divided by squared mean) of the interarrival and service times, and $\rho=\lambda_{\text{call}}\mathbb{E}[T_s]<1$ for utilization.

For this server, the **Kingman approximation**\index{Kingman approximation!definition}[^fn-kingman-heavy-traffic] [@kingman1961single] estimates the mean time waiting *before* service:

$$\mathbb{E}[W_q] \approx \frac{c_a^2+c_s^2}{2}\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}\mathbb{E}[T_s].$$ {#eq-vol3-kingman-gg1}

[^fn-scv-arrival-burstiness]: **Squared Coefficient of Variation**: The scale-free measure of burstiness. Exponential interarrival or service times, as in a Poisson stream, have a squared coefficient of variation of exactly one, and perfectly regular ones have zero, so the notebook's values above one describe arrivals and service times burstier than Poisson, which is the usual state of agent traffic that arrives in cohorts and makes calls of very different lengths.

[^fn-kingman-heavy-traffic]: **Heavy Traffic**: Kingman's 1961 note showed that as load approaches one, the steady-state waiting time of the single-server queue, suitably scaled, converges to an exponential distribution [@kingman1961single]. The consequence reaches past the mean: near saturation the whole waiting-time distribution, and with it every percentile, stretches by the same $\rho/(1-\rho)$ factor, so a latency target set as a percentile degrades as fast as the mean does.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_economics_queue_wait_margin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Curve of mean wait against utilization that stays low and then rises steeply. A blue dot at 70 percent utilization is labeled 7 seconds and a red dot at 90 percent is labeled 27 seconds."}

*Near saturation, a little more utilization buys a lot more waiting.*
:::

The factor $\rho/(1-\rho)$ is why waiting grows so fast near full utilization; the expression is a heavy-traffic approximation to the mean, not an exact mean or a percentile. A derivation and error analysis are given by @boon2023heavy. Correlated agent bursts, batched inference, worker pools, and shared quotas need models or trace-driven simulations that represent them, and substituting a pooled service rate does not turn this equation into a multi-server one.

::: {#nbk-18-sizing-queue-capacity-and-tail .callout-notebook title="Pricing mean queue delay"}

**Problem**: In the hypothetical single-server model above, mean service takes `{python} QueuePrice.service_str`, $c_a^2$ is `{python} QueuePrice.ca2_str`, and $c_s^2$ is `{python} QueuePrice.cs2_str`. A waiting call holds resources costing `{python} QueuePrice.holding_rate_str` per second. How do estimated mean wait and holding cost change between `{python} QueuePrice.rho_low_str` and `{python} QueuePrice.rho_high_str` utilization?

**Math**: Use @eq-vol3-kingman-gg1, then multiply mean wait by the stated linear holding rate. The rate covers only resources retained during the queue interval, excluding model service, tool execution, and any separate valuation of user delay.

**Result**: Estimated mean wait rises from `{python} QueuePrice.wait_low_str` to `{python} QueuePrice.wait_high_str`, and the corresponding holding charge rises from `{python} QueuePrice.holding_low_str` to `{python} QueuePrice.holding_high_str` per call.

**Systems insight**: Moving from `{python} QueuePrice.rho_low_str` to `{python} QueuePrice.rho_high_str` utilization buys `{python} QueuePrice.throughput_gain_str` more throughput from the same server and multiplies mean wait by `{python} QueuePrice.wait_ratio_mult_str`, because the $\rho/(1-\rho)$ factor, not the service time, dominates near saturation. The holding charge per call stays small; the wait itself, repeated on every serial call of a trajectory, is the cost. Halving the variability term $(c_a^2+c_s^2)/2$, for example by smoothing bursty admissions, halves the wait at any utilization and is the cheaper lever before buying reserve capacity. The reserve itself is sized from measured latency percentiles.

:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-tail-compounding
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SERIAL TAIL COMPOUNDING ALONG A TRAJECTORY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-agent-economics-capacity, after the queue-price notebook.
# │ Goal: Show why good per-call tails still give routinely slow trajectories.
# │ Show: Probability that at least one of n serial calls meets a p99 delay.
# │ How:  1 - (1 - p)^n under independent per-call tail events.
# │ Note: Scenario call count; p is the definition of a 99th percentile.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int

class TailCompounding:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Scenario inputs) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    n_calls = 30  # scenario: serial model calls on the trajectory's path
    p_tail = 0.01  # a call exceeds its own p99 latency with probability 0.01

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    p_hit = 1 - (1 - p_tail) ** n_calls

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < p_tail < 1 and n_calls >= 1, "Valid tail probability and call count")
    check(p_tail < p_hit < n_calls * p_tail, "Compounding exceeds one call and stays below the union bound")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_calls_str = fmt_int(n_calls)
    p_tail_str = fmt(p_tail, precision=2)
    p_hit_str = fmt(p_hit, precision=2)
```

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_economics_tail_compounding_margin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Rising curve of the probability of meeting at least one per-call tail delay against the number of serial calls, approaching a dashed line labeled certain. A red dot at 30 calls is labeled 0.26."}

*A one-in-a-hundred delay per call becomes routine across a long trajectory.*
:::

Means also hide how tails compound along a trajectory. If each of $n$ serial calls independently exceeds its 99th-percentile latency with probability $p_{\text{tail}}$, the trajectory meets at least one such delay with probability $1-(1-p_{\text{tail}})^n$, the horizon compounding of @sec-vol3-intro-horizon-arithmetic applied to latency. A trajectory of `{python} TailCompounding.n_calls_str` serial calls, each with tail probability `{python} TailCompounding.p_tail_str`, meets at least one tail delay with probability `{python} TailCompounding.p_hit_str`. A fleet sized for good per-call latency therefore still delivers slow trajectories routinely. This is the serial counterpart of the fan-out straggler effect in @sec-vol3-multiagent-backpressure [@dean2013tail]. Correlated delays, such as a shared queue that stays long across consecutive calls, change the probability but not the lesson: provision and schedule against trajectory-level percentiles, not per-call means (principle \ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-goodput}).

The queueing model completes the routing rule of @sec-vol3-agent-economics-cascades. The router compares eligible *remaining paths*, including their queue and service delays, retained-resource costs, verification, and escalation, under the same acceptance contract. Rerouting changes the arrival rates that produced the delay estimate, so the estimate is refreshed after each routing change. Separating interactive and batch capacity, or scheduling by priority, protects latency-bound work at a cost in fairness and utilization that is measured like any other.

### Dedicated capacity versus per-token APIs

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-breakeven
#| echo: false
from mlsysim import *

class DedicatedBreakEven:
    # 1. LOAD: hypothetical matched-capability comparison; dollars and
    # token counts are scalar accounting units, time remains a quantity.
    input_per_output = 5.0
    cached_share = 0.80
    input_per_million, cached_per_million, output_per_million = 3.0, 0.30, 15.0
    fixed_per_hour = 28.0
    variable_per_million = 2.0
    reference_rate = 1_200 / second
    load_fraction = 0.52

    # 2. EXECUTE
    weighted_input = (1 - cached_share) * input_per_million + cached_share * cached_per_million
    api_per_million = output_per_million + input_per_output * weighted_input
    reference_hour_tokens = (reference_rate * hour).to(ureg.dimensionless).magnitude
    delivered_hour_tokens = load_fraction * reference_hour_tokens
    api_hour = delivered_hour_tokens * api_per_million / 1_000_000
    dedicated_hour = fixed_per_hour + delivered_hour_tokens * variable_per_million / 1_000_000
    contribution_hour = reference_hour_tokens * (api_per_million - variable_per_million) / 1_000_000
    crossing = fixed_per_hour / contribution_hour
    saving_hour = api_hour - dedicated_hour
    # Sensitivity: the same workload with no cached input on the API side.
    api_nocache_per_million = output_per_million + input_per_output * input_per_million
    crossing_nocache = fixed_per_hour / (reference_hour_tokens * (api_nocache_per_million - variable_per_million) / 1_000_000)

    # 3. GUARD
    check(0 <= cached_share <= 1 and 0 < load_fraction <= 1, "Valid mix and load")
    check(reference_rate > 0 / second and fixed_per_hour > 0, "Positive capacity and commitment")
    check(
        input_per_output >= 0 and min(input_per_million, cached_per_million, output_per_million, variable_per_million) >= 0,
        "Nonnegative prices and mix",
    )
    check(api_per_million > variable_per_million and 0 < crossing < load_fraction, "This scenario crosses below its operating load")
    check(saving_hour > 0, "Dedicated cost is lower at the assumed load")
    check(crossing_nocache < crossing, "Cache discounts on the API raise the crossing")

    # 4. OUTPUT
    input_per_output_str = fmt(input_per_output, precision=0)
    cached_share_str = fmt_percent(cached_share, precision=0, style="prose")
    input_price_str = fmt_usd(input_per_million, precision=0)
    cached_price_str = fmt_usd(cached_per_million, precision=1)
    output_price_str = fmt_usd(output_per_million, precision=0)
    fixed_str = fmt_usd(fixed_per_hour, precision=0)
    variable_str = fmt_usd(variable_per_million, precision=0)
    rate_str = fmt_rate(reference_rate.to(1 / second).magnitude, "tokens/s", precision=0, commas=True)
    load_str = fmt_percent(load_fraction, precision=0, style="prose")
    weighted_input_str = fmt_usd(weighted_input, precision=2)
    api_price_str = fmt_usd(api_per_million, precision=1)
    crossing_str = fmt_percent(crossing, precision=1, style="prose")
    delivered_str = fmt_int(round(delivered_hour_tokens))
    api_hour_str = fmt_usd(api_hour, precision=2)
    dedicated_hour_str = fmt_usd(dedicated_hour, precision=2)
    saving_str = fmt_usd(saving_hour, precision=2)
    crossing_nocache_str = fmt_percent(crossing_nocache, precision=1, style="prose")
```

Once a workload's token bill is large and steady, a team can run its own deployment instead of paying per token, at a hypothetical `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.fixed_str` per hour plus `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.variable_str` per million output tokens. That deployment is **dedicated capacity**\index{Dedicated capacity!definition}, a commitment paid whether its resources are busy or idle, so the decision turns on how much of its capacity the workload keeps busy.[^fn-cloud-utilization-argument] The comparison is a matched one, with equivalent effective capability, acceptance criteria, privacy and authority constraints, and feasible latency at the workload mix; a similar model name or token rate does not establish that equivalence.

Fix the input/output and cache mix. Let $p_{\mathrm{API}}$ be the API charge per output token *including its associated input*, $p_{\mathrm{ded}}$ the deployment's variable charge per output token, and $C_{\mathrm{fixed}}$ its complete hourly fixed cost, including provisioned idle and reserve capacity, amortized operations, and other costs that differ between the alternatives. Common costs cancel only if they are genuinely unchanged; a differing tool, verification, networking, or support cost belongs in the comparison. Let $\mu_{\mathrm{out}}$ be a measured feasible output rate, in tokens per second, for this mix and latency target, and let $u$ be the fraction of that reference capacity the workload delivers, which is not accelerator busy time. An hour then delivers $3600\mu_{\mathrm{out}}u$ output tokens, which cost $3600\mu_{\mathrm{out}}u\,p_{\mathrm{API}}$ through an API with no fixed fee and $C_{\mathrm{fixed}}+3600\mu_{\mathrm{out}}u\,p_{\mathrm{ded}}$ on dedicated capacity. When $p_{\mathrm{API}}>p_{\mathrm{ded}}$, the two costs cross at the **break-even utilization**\index{Break-even utilization!definition}

$$u^* = \frac{C_{\mathrm{fixed}}}{3600\mu_{\mathrm{out}}(p_{\mathrm{API}}-p_{\mathrm{ded}})}.$$ {#eq-vol3-breakeven-utilization}

[^fn-cloud-utilization-argument]: **Pay-as-You-Go Economics**: The same comparison drove the economics of cloud computing. Renting capacity by the hour can cost less than owning it even at a higher hourly price, because owned capacity is paid for at its average utilization and the renter transfers the risk of over- and under-provisioning to the provider [@armbrust2010view]. A per-token API is that argument taken to its finest grain, which is why the crossing $u^*$, not the list price, decides the purchase.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_economics_breakeven_margin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two cost-per-hour lines against delivered load. A red per-token API line starts at zero and rises steeply; a blue dedicated line starts at a fixed cost and rises gently. They cross at a dot above a dashed marker labeled u star."}

*Owned capacity wins only above the load that repays its fixed cost.*
:::

If $u^*>1$, the dedicated alternative cannot reach the crossing within the stated capacity; if $p_{\mathrm{API}}\le p_{\mathrm{ded}}$ and $C_{\mathrm{fixed}}>0$, it never becomes cheaper. Deadlines and quotas are checked separately at the chosen load.

::: {#nbk-18-financial-break-even-utilization-for-dedicated .callout-notebook title="Pricing idle capacity and cached input"}

**Problem**: Assume a hypothetical matched-capability workload uses `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.input_per_output_str` input tokens per output token, with `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.cached_share_str` of inputs billed at the cached rate. API prices per million tokens are `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.input_price_str` for uncached input, `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.cached_price_str` for cached input, and `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.output_price_str` for output. A dedicated deployment costs `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.fixed_str` per hour for its entire provisioned capacity and operations, plus `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.variable_str` per million output tokens for all remaining differential variable costs. Its feasible reference output rate is assumed to be `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.rate_str` under the same mix, reserve policy, and latency target. Which alternative costs less at `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.load_str` of that rate?

**Math**: Weight the two input prices by the billed token fractions, then include associated input in $p_{\mathrm{API}}$. Apply @eq-vol3-breakeven-utilization. Both alternatives are assumed feasible at this operating point, and common tool, assessment, and other unchanged task costs cancel. The prices are scenario inputs, not current provider prices.

**Result**: Weighted input costs `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.weighted_input_str` per million input tokens. Including associated input, the API costs `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.api_price_str` per million output tokens. The cost crossing is `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.crossing_str` of reference capacity. At the stated load, `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.delivered_str` output tokens per hour cost `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.api_hour_str` through the API and `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.dedicated_hour_str` on dedicated capacity, a difference of `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.saving_str` per hour.

**Systems insight**: The crossing moves with the API's effective price per output token. Without cached input the same workload would cross at `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.crossing_nocache_str` of reference capacity instead of `{python} DedicatedBreakEven.crossing_str`, because heavy prefix reuse on the API side erodes the case for owning capacity. Commit to dedicated capacity only when sustained load stays above $u^*$ with the reserve the latency target requires, since idle hours below the crossing are paid at the full fixed rate; ownership keeps queueing, failures, and quotas on the team's side of the ledger.

:::

::: {#chk-18-mlfq-scheduling .callout-checkpoint title="Check the capacity boundary"}

Before bounding what one trajectory may spend, check the capacity model.

- [ ] **Residence vs. service**: Why can mean trajectory concurrency be high while model-worker occupancy is low?
- [ ] **Queue headroom**: With the variability in notebook \ref{nbk-18-sizing-queue-capacity-and-tail}, what utilization keeps the estimated mean wait below one mean service time? What changes if arrivals come in correlated batches?
- [ ] **Acceptance and load**: If a model change lowers acceptance while goodput is held fixed, how does $\rho(\alpha)$ change, and at what relative drop does the fleet in notebook \ref{nbk-18-trajectory-residence-and-quota} exhaust its token quota?
- [ ] **Cache and crossing**: Why can cached-input pricing move the dedicated/API crossing without changing a provider's token quota?

:::

Capacity planning prices the resources needed to sustain admitted work. Limiting what one trajectory and its descendants may spend takes an admission and settlement ledger, which the next section develops.

## Spending Governance {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-governance}

A coordinator can admit two children against the same free balance if each checks that balance before either records its reservation. Both local checks pass, yet the combined liability exceeds the task allowance. Cancellation introduces a second race. Returning a stopped child's allocation while its remote call remains billable lets another child spend money already committed elsewhere. The admission rule from @sec-vol3-controlplane-accounting must therefore remain conserved across concurrent allocations, crashes, and late settlement.

### Bound liability before admitting work

Let $E(t)$ denote gross charges settled into a task's ledger and $R(t)$ the funds withheld there for outstanding liabilities, delegated allocations, and protected finalization. A task with authorized budget $B_{\text{task}}$ maintains

$$E(t)+R(t)\le B_{\text{task}}.$$

Before admitting an operation, the runtime reserves a bound $\bar c$ on its additional charge, not its expected cost. That bound covers the billing categories in the declared account. For a model call, input size and the service-enforced output allowance must cover every billable token category at the applicable rates. A tool or rented resource may also require an enforced duration, data-volume, or total-charge limit. Charges during stopping and required cleanup need backing too. A host timeout or an estimated mean cost leaves a service free to keep billing, so under a hard-ceiling policy the runtime refuses such an operation or uses a bounded alternative; a threshold with possible overshoot is a different contract.

The bound also depends on complete mediation. Shared credentials that let a worker bypass the reservation gate defeat the ledger, as do billable retries omitted from its records. A cache discount lowers settlement, and it lowers the initial reservation only when the service guarantees the discount for the admitted request.

The account here measures gross charges. Releasing an unused reservation restores permission to spend money that was never charged. A later provider credit or refund is a separate recorded adjustment that leaves gross spending and this authorization unchanged. New budget comes only from an operator's explicit allocation, never automatically from a recovery or a promising new candidate.

### Conserve the allocation across descendants

Each node $k$ keeps the same account in a runtime-owned ledger, with allocation $B_k$, settled gross charges $E_k$, reservations $R_k$, and free balance $F_k$. The local conservation rule is

$$B_k=E_k+R_k+F_k,\qquad E_k,R_k,F_k\ge0.$$

A **budget reservation**\index{Budget reservation!definition}[^fn-escrow-budget-reservation] removes funds from $F_k$ before another operation can claim them. A child's allocation remains reserved at its parent while the child spends within its own ledger. Parent and child records therefore represent the same backing at different levels, not additional money. Summing every node's reserved balance would double-count it. The parent's $E_k$ alone also omits charges still held in open child accounts. Fleet reporting attributes each charge once through its operation record, while the hierarchy accounts for which allocation backs it.

The updates in @tbl-vol3-ledger-transitions are atomic with respect to competing admissions and control changes. Their records must survive the failure domain declared in @sec-vol3-persistence-wal before billable work can leave the runtime. A replacement owner reconstructs reservations from that history rather than resetting a balance because the former worker disappeared. Permission grants remain separate from these consumed allocations. Delegating permission to read a repository does not subtract that permission from the parent; delegating spending capacity withholds funds the parent otherwise could use.

| Ledger event                           | Required condition                                                        | Conserved update                                                                 |
|:---------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Allocate $b$ to a child                | Current authority and eligibility; $b\le F_P$                             | Parent moves $b$ from $F_P$ to $R_P$; child starts with $B_C=F_C=b$              |
| Admit an operation bounded by $\bar c$ | Current guards pass; $\bar c\le F_k$                                      | Move $\bar c$ from $F_k$ to $R_k$ and record the operation and attempt binding   |
| Final settlement with charge $c$       | Authenticated final evidence; $0\le c\le \bar c$; reservation still owned | Remove $\bar c$ from $R_k$, add $c$ to $E_k$, and return $\bar c-c$ to $F_k$     |
| Stop a child with unsettled work       | New admission is closed; outstanding records remain owned                 | Keep backing for its calls and descendants; stopping alone releases no liability |
| Close a fully settled child            | No further admission; calls and descendants settled; $R_C=0$              | Parent removes $B_C$ from $R_P$, adds $E_C$ to $E_P$, and adds $F_C$ to $F_P$    |

: **Conserved budget transitions**: Each update preserves the allocated total. Closure requires financial settlement, not merely a stopped local process. {#tbl-vol3-ledger-transitions}

[^fn-escrow-budget-reservation]: **Escrow**: Databases solved the same concurrency problem for hot aggregate quantities such as account balances and inventory counts. The escrow transactional method lets long-lived transactions set aside part of an aggregate instead of locking it, so other transactions keep updating the remainder and commits of different updates can proceed asynchronously [@oneil1986escrow]. A budget reservation is escrow applied to spending authority, with the provider's final bill playing the role of the commit.

Reservation identity binds the task, logical operation, transport attempt, price basis, and cost bound. Settlement uses authenticated usage evidence and a durable **settlement identity**\index{Settlement identity!definition}, the key under which one final charge is applied to the ledger. Repeated delivery of the same evidence applies the ledger update at most once; the runtime checks that a reused identity has the same payload. A conflicting amount is a reconciliation fault, not another charge to add or a duplicate to ignore. Partial usage can move known charges into $E_k$ while retaining a bound on all remaining liability; the full reservation is released only at finality. Deduplicating an effect at its endpoint and deduplicating a billing record are different contracts.

If a reported charge exceeds its reservation, the ledger's assumed upper bound has failed. Clamping the charge or making free balance negative would conceal that failure. The runtime records the discrepancy, holds further affected admission, and escalates reconciliation, and the hard guarantee lapses until reconciliation restores it. With valid charge bounds, atomic admission, and correct settlement, each transition preserves nonnegative balances and prevents a child from spending outside its backing.

### Cancellation does not close the account

The cancellation boundary from @sec-vol3-multiagent-backpressure stops new work where current control is enforced, but remote termination and final billing can arrive later. A child's allocation remains held until those obligations settle. If retaining the child ledger is inconvenient, a durable transfer can move its known charges, outstanding reservations, and genuinely free balance to an authorized settlement owner. The transfer preserves operation identities and backing, including allocations held by unfinished descendants. No interval may exist in which both owners can release the same funds, or neither owns the liability.

Protected finalization has its own reservation within the same budget. The runtime can use that allowance for scoped status queries and cleanup after ordinary admission stops; it does not revive the child's grant. A terminal task may retain an unsettled account or transfer it, and a report at a cutoff separates settled charges from outstanding liability. The notebook traces this distinction for a canceled child with a late final bill.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-ledger
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONSERVED BUDGET WITH A CANCELED CHILD AND A LATE BILL
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-agent-economics-governance and its ledger notebook.
# │ Goal: Keep a stopped child's remote liability backed until final settlement.
# │ Show: Root balances, child pending liability, late bill, and released funds.
# │ How: Exact integer accounting in thousandths of a scenario dollar, followed
# │      by the atomic transfers of @tbl-vol3-ledger-transitions.
# │ Note: Hypothetical charge records and enforceable bounds, not provider rates.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_usd

class BudgetLedger:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Hypothetical records; integer milli-dollars) ─────────────
    units_per_dollar = 1000
    b_root = 5000
    c_plan = 42  # final planning charge already settled at the first row
    b_trace, b_fuzz = 1200, 2500
    e_trace, e_fuzz = 380, 850
    pending_fuzz = 1000  # enforceable maximum remaining remote charge
    late_charge = 700  # authenticated final bill received after local stop

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Conserved transitions) ───────────────────────────────
    f_after_plan = b_root - c_plan
    r_deleg = b_trace + b_fuzz
    f_after_deleg = f_after_plan - r_deleg
    refund_trace = b_trace - e_trace
    e_after_trace = c_plan + e_trace
    r_after_trace = r_deleg - b_trace
    f_after_trace = f_after_deleg + refund_trace
    fuzz_free_at_stop = b_fuzz - e_fuzz - pending_fuzz
    fuzz_apparent_free = b_fuzz - e_fuzz  # what a release at local stop would return
    settlement_records = (("fuzz_final_bill", late_charge), ("fuzz_final_bill", late_charge))  # duplicate delivery
    applied_settlements = {}
    fuzz_e_settled = e_fuzz
    for settlement_id, reported_charge in settlement_records:
        if settlement_id in applied_settlements:
            check(applied_settlements[settlement_id] == reported_charge, "Conflicting payload for a settlement identity")
        else:
            applied_settlements[settlement_id] = reported_charge
            fuzz_e_settled += reported_charge
    fuzz_free_settled = fuzz_free_at_stop + pending_fuzz - late_charge
    e_final = e_after_trace + fuzz_e_settled
    r_final = r_after_trace - b_fuzz
    f_final = f_after_trace + fuzz_free_settled
    root_states = (
        (c_plan, 0, f_after_plan),
        (c_plan, r_deleg, f_after_deleg),
        (e_after_trace, r_after_trace, f_after_trace),
        (e_after_trace, r_after_trace, f_after_trace),
        (e_final, r_final, f_final),
    )

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Conservation and displayed claims) ──────────────────────
    for settled, reserved, free in root_states:
        check(settled + reserved + free == b_root, "Root conservation failed")
        check(min(settled, reserved, free) >= 0, "Negative ledger balance")
    check(e_fuzz + pending_fuzz + fuzz_free_at_stop == b_fuzz, "Stopped child must retain the remote reservation")
    check(0 <= late_charge <= pending_fuzz, "Late bill must fit its enforced bound")
    check(root_states[2] == root_states[3], "Local stop must not release backing")
    check(e_final == c_plan + e_trace + e_fuzz + late_charge == 1972, "Every final charge must enter exactly once")
    check(f_final == 3028 and r_final == 0, "Final free balance drift")
    check(fuzz_free_at_stop == 650 and fuzz_free_settled == 950, "Late settlement releases only the unused part")
    check(fuzz_apparent_free - fuzz_free_at_stop == pending_fuzz > late_charge, "Premature release overcommits the bound")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Dollar strings) ───────────────────────────────────────
    b_root_str = fmt_usd(b_root / units_per_dollar, precision=0)
    c_plan_str = fmt_usd(c_plan / units_per_dollar, precision=3)
    b_trace_str = fmt_usd(b_trace / units_per_dollar, precision=2)
    b_fuzz_str = fmt_usd(b_fuzz / units_per_dollar, precision=2)
    e_trace_str = fmt_usd(e_trace / units_per_dollar, precision=2)
    e_fuzz_str = fmt_usd(e_fuzz / units_per_dollar, precision=2)
    pending_fuzz_str = fmt_usd(pending_fuzz / units_per_dollar, precision=0)
    late_charge_str = fmt_usd(late_charge / units_per_dollar, precision=2)
    f_after_plan_str = fmt_usd(f_after_plan / units_per_dollar, precision=3)
    r_deleg_str = fmt_usd(r_deleg / units_per_dollar, precision=2)
    f_after_deleg_str = fmt_usd(f_after_deleg / units_per_dollar, precision=3)
    e_after_trace_str = fmt_usd(e_after_trace / units_per_dollar, precision=3)
    r_after_trace_str = fmt_usd(r_after_trace / units_per_dollar, precision=2)
    f_after_trace_str = fmt_usd(f_after_trace / units_per_dollar, precision=3)
    fuzz_free_at_stop_str = fmt_usd(fuzz_free_at_stop / units_per_dollar, precision=2)
    fuzz_free_settled_str = fmt_usd(fuzz_free_settled / units_per_dollar, precision=2)
    e_final_str = fmt_usd(e_final / units_per_dollar, precision=3)
    r_final_str = fmt_usd(r_final / units_per_dollar, precision=0)
    f_final_str = fmt_usd(f_final / units_per_dollar, precision=3)
    fuzz_apparent_free_str = fmt_usd(fuzz_apparent_free / units_per_dollar, precision=2)
```

::: {#nbk-18-hierarchical-multi-agent-budget-allocation-and .callout-notebook title="A canceled child with a late bill"}

**Problem**: A hypothetical repair has a `{python} BudgetLedger.b_root_str` budget. Its planning charge has settled at `{python} BudgetLedger.c_plan_str`, and it allocates `{python} BudgetLedger.b_trace_str` to trace analysis and `{python} BudgetLedger.b_fuzz_str` to fuzzing. The trace child closes with a final charge of `{python} BudgetLedger.e_trace_str`. The fuzzing child has settled `{python} BudgetLedger.e_fuzz_str` and holds `{python} BudgetLedger.pending_fuzz_str` for a remote operation when its local executor confirms termination. No further child work is admitted. The remote operation later terminates with a final additional bill of `{python} BudgetLedger.late_charge_str`. All other charges and required finalization are included in these records, and neither child has descendants. When can the root release the fuzzing allocation?

**Math**: We keep the entire child allocation reserved at the root until its account closes. @Tbl-vol3-late-bill-ledger follows the root's balances under the same conservation rule throughout.

| Root ledger boundary                    |                               Settled $E$ |                              Reserved $R$ |                                  Free $F$ |
|:----------------------------------------|------------------------------------------:|------------------------------------------:|------------------------------------------:|
| Planning settled                        |        `{python} BudgetLedger.c_plan_str` |       `{python} BudgetLedger.r_final_str` |  `{python} BudgetLedger.f_after_plan_str` |
| Both allocations granted                |        `{python} BudgetLedger.c_plan_str` |       `{python} BudgetLedger.r_deleg_str` | `{python} BudgetLedger.f_after_deleg_str` |
| Trace child closed                      | `{python} BudgetLedger.e_after_trace_str` | `{python} BudgetLedger.r_after_trace_str` | `{python} BudgetLedger.f_after_trace_str` |
| Fuzzing locally stopped; bill pending   | `{python} BudgetLedger.e_after_trace_str` | `{python} BudgetLedger.r_after_trace_str` | `{python} BudgetLedger.f_after_trace_str` |
| Late bill settled; fuzzing child closed |       `{python} BudgetLedger.e_final_str` |       `{python} BudgetLedger.r_final_str` |       `{python} BudgetLedger.f_final_str` |

: **Root Balances Through a Late Bill**: Local stopping retains the pending child's allocation until its charges settle and its account closes. {#tbl-vol3-late-bill-ledger}

At local termination, the fuzzing ledger has `{python} BudgetLedger.fuzz_free_at_stop_str` free, but its remote reservation remains outstanding. Final settlement releases the unused part of that reservation, leaving `{python} BudgetLedger.fuzz_free_settled_str` to return when the child closes. Re-delivery of the same final billing record changes none of these balances.

**Systems insight**: A release at local stop would have returned `{python} BudgetLedger.fuzz_apparent_free_str`, the allocation minus settled charges, when only `{python} BudgetLedger.fuzz_free_at_stop_str` was free; the `{python} BudgetLedger.late_charge_str` bill would then have landed on funds already promised to another child. The rule at stop is to release at most the allocation minus settled charges minus the enforceable bound on outstanding work, and to release the rest only as each bound settles. The guarantee is exactly as strong as those bounds and the completeness of the records.

:::

@Fig-vol3-hierarchical-budget-ledger draws the same accounts at both levels of the tree. The root's bars keep one length because every transition moves funds among settled, reserved, and free balances without creating or losing any.

::: {#fig-vol3-hierarchical-budget-ledger fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Conservation Across a Canceled Child**: Top, the root allocates to two children, and the fuzzing child's ledger at local stop splits its allocation into settled charges, a pending remote reservation, and free balance. Bottom, the root's balances at each boundary of @tbl-vol3-late-bill-ledger always sum to the same budget. Local stopping leaves the root's reservation unchanged; only settlement of the late bill moves the fuzzing allocation into settled and free balances." fig-alt="Top: a root ledger box with arrows to a trace child box and a fuzzing child box. The fuzzing child box contains a stacked bar with settled, pending remote, and free segments and a note about the late bill. Bottom: five equal-length stacked bars, one per root ledger boundary, divided into settled, reserved, and free segments, with the settled amount listed in a column at the right. The fourth bar, labeled fuzzing stopped, bill pending, matches the third."}
![](images/svg/hierarchical-budget-ledger.svg)
:::

### Separate spending alarms from admission limits

A cumulative allowance can still permit an undesirable burst of work. A retrospective **spending alarm**\index{Spending alarm!definition} watches the charge rate, the charges that entered the account over a trailing window of duration $\tau$ divided by $\tau$. Delayed billing can make it spike after execution has stopped, or stay low while several expensive calls are in flight. It can trigger investigation or a hold on new work; the spending it measured has already happened.

An **admission limit**\index{Admission limit!definition} instead checks newly admitted financial commitments, as reservations, before dispatch. For an allowance $B_\tau$ over each trailing window of duration $\tau$, one conservative policy requires

$$\sum_{i:\,t-\tau<t_i\le t}\bar c_i\le B_\tau,$$

where $t_i$ is the admission time and $\bar c_i$ the bounded charge of a billable operation.[^fn-window-token-bucket] Every admission atomically checks this window as well as the cumulative ledger. The window covers all children in its scope, not a fresh full allowance for each child. Moving an allocation down the tree is not a second billable operation. Keeping $\bar c_i$ in the window until its admission ages out avoids treating early completion as permission for an unlimited burst. This bounds admitted commitments in that interval, not when providers execute them or post their bills; actual billing can bunch later.

[^fn-window-token-bucket]: **Trailing Window versus Token Bucket**: A token bucket, the usual network and API rate limiter, admits a burst up to its depth at once and then a sustained rate, so its worst case over a short interval is the depth plus the rate times the interval. The trailing-window sum caps every window of length $\tau$ at $B_\tau$ directly, whatever shape the burst takes, at the cost of keeping each admission's record until it ages out.

Rate controls must also leave capacity and funding for required finalization, or a stop can starve the status queries needed to settle its own reservations. Protected lanes or explicit finalization allowances inside the same total account solve that, and a successful probe or cleared alert never releases unrelated held funds.

Repeated failures or unchanged candidate artifacts can trigger a spending hold under the watchdog policy of @sec-vol3-sagas-watchdogs. The hold bounds the experiment without judging it. The runtime applies the declared stop or escalation policy and keeps its liabilities, and the acceptance contract, not the budget, decides whether the work produced a useful result.

Reservations make an architectural comparison enforceable under stated billing and failure assumptions. With cost, latency, and liability accounted for, the remaining decision is whether a fixed workflow, a model call, or a bounded delegated loop earns its additional expense on the target task.

## Pricing the Choice of Architecture {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-selection}

A spending bound makes a proposed architecture admissible under its budget, and the account decides whether it is worth buying. We can now compare deterministic code, a fixed model-assisted workflow, a bounded loop, and delegation using the same acceptance contract and complete account. The objective comes first. Minimizing cost subject to a completion requirement can select a different design from minimizing deadline misses under a spending ceiling.

### Compare designs, not an autonomy ranking {#sec-vol3-selection-spectrum}

The alternatives differ in who chooses the next step, as @tbl-vol3-architecture-spectrum shows, and that ordering says nothing about cost, latency, or permitted effects. An expensive fixed workflow can cost more than a short adaptive loop, parallel work can lower elapsed time while raising aggregate spend, and a single model call can still propose an irreversible action that needs authorization.

| Design                        | Who selects the next operation                       | Incremental obligation to price                                                     |
|:------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Deterministic program         | Program control flow                                 | Maintenance, execution, assessment, and exception handling                          |
| Fixed model-assisted workflow | Program control flow around model calls              | Model usage, output validation, and fallback paths                                  |
| Bounded model-directed loop   | Model proposals admitted by the runtime              | Repeated observations, revision, stopping, and effect settlement                    |
| Delegated trajectories        | Coordinator and children within assignment contracts | Child execution, communication, integration, cancellation, and residual liabilities |

: **Architecture Choices Under One Task Contract**: The control structure changes the work to account for, not the required acceptance evidence or authorized effects. {#tbl-vol3-architecture-spectrum}

Every design can carry state, need recovery, and need substantive verification. The matched comparison holds the acceptance contract fixed across designs, neither relaxing it for a single call nor tightening it for delegation.

### Price the task's obligations {#sec-vol3-selection-questions}

Horizon, state, and authority identify obligations to price; they are not a classifier that chooses an architecture. A longer horizon creates more opportunities to consume resources and meet failures, priced by the steps the policy actually reaches. State incurs retrieval, retention, consistency, and recovery work wherever it lives. An adaptive loop earns its extra observations when they improve the decision enough to repay their cost.

Authority determines which effects need admission, evidence, and settlement. Irreversible effects need an authorization and risk policy, which may include human approval, and unresolved effects keep their reservations in the account whatever the expected bill.

Closure evidence determines what additional attempts can establish. An executable check supplies inexpensive, specific feedback, with its coverage and false-accept behavior part of the comparison. Where no such check exists, further observations, independent sources, or expert review can still improve a result, and their measured value enters the account like any other. Human review has its own cost, delay, and error rate, and a task routed to a person counts as completed only when the person completes it under the contract.

### Economic feasibility envelopes for agentic loops {#sec-vol3-selection-economics}

A dependency-upgrade service can run a rule-based rewriter, a single model call, or a cheaper model that retries for up to three turns before a person takes over. The single call and the rewriter each have one acceptance rate; the loop's rate and cost depend on how many turns it actually reaches. For a bounded loop, let $q_k$ be the probability that turn $k$ produces an accepted result conditional on reaching it after earlier rejections. Assume each reached turn receives a completed assessment, the loop stops at acceptance, and otherwise continues up to $K$ turns. Then

$$p_{\text{loop}}(K) = 1 - \prod_{k=1}^K (1 - q_k)$$ {#eq-vol3-loop-success}

As in the cascade, this is the probability chain rule, not an independence assumption. Turn $k$ is reached with probability $r_k=\prod_{j<k}(1-q_j)$, where $r_1=1$. If $c_k$ includes all charges for that reached turn, including assessment and holding resources, the expected automated cost per incoming ticket is $\sum_{k=1}^K r_k c_k$. With equal turn cost, this becomes that cost times $\sum_k r_k$, the expected number of turns. Assessment outages or a separate abandonment policy require additional branches; they cannot be silently treated as ordinary rejections.

The denominator changes when human completion enters the policy. For automated acceptance probability $p$, expected automated cost $c$, and one human fallback costing $C_h$ with conditional resolution probability $h$ after automated rejection, expected combined spend per incoming ticket is $c+(1-p)C_h$. The combined resolution probability is $p+(1-p)h$. Dividing the former by the latter prices a resolved ticket under the combined policy, whereas $c/p$ prices an automated acceptance before human fallback. Neither ratio is finite when its acceptance denominator is zero. The following example keeps these accounts separate.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-architecture
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DEPENDENCY-UPGRADE ARCHITECTURE CHOICE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-18-architectural-frontier-migration-under-cost.
# │ Goal: Compare automation alone with a policy including human completion.
# │ Show: Conditional loop yield, all assessed costs, and resolved-ticket costs.
# │ How: Weight reached turns; price one fallback; keep denominators separate.
# │ Scope: Hypothetical population expectations, not observed benchmark data.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import USD
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_usd, fmt_percent

class ArchitectureChoice:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    tickets = 10_000  # illustrative monthly arrivals
    c_rules = 0.001 * USD  # all automated charges except the common assessment
    c_call = 0.045 * USD
    c_turn = 0.006 * USD
    c_ver = 0.002 * USD  # same acceptance assessment for every candidate
    p_rules, p_call = 0.32, 0.68
    r1, r2, r3 = 0.55, 0.42, 0.30
    c_human = 35 * USD  # one fallback, including its final assessment
    human_resolution = 0.90  # conditional on entering human fallback
    resolution_floor = 0.95  # declared combined-policy requirement

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    reach2 = 1 - r1
    reach3 = reach2 * (1 - r2)
    p_loop = 1 - reach3 * (1 - r3)
    turns = 1 + reach2 + reach3
    auto_rules = c_rules + c_ver
    auto_call = c_call + c_ver
    auto_loop = turns * (c_turn + c_ver)
    auto_per_rules = auto_rules / p_rules
    auto_per_call = auto_call / p_call
    auto_per_loop = auto_loop / p_loop
    total_rules = auto_rules + (1 - p_rules) * c_human
    total_call = auto_call + (1 - p_call) * c_human
    total_loop = auto_loop + (1 - p_loop) * c_human
    resolved_rules = p_rules + (1 - p_rules) * human_resolution
    resolved_call = p_call + (1 - p_call) * human_resolution
    resolved_loop = p_loop + (1 - p_loop) * human_resolution
    per_rules = total_rules / resolved_rules
    per_call = total_call / resolved_call
    per_loop = total_loop / resolved_loop
    month_loop = tickets * total_loop
    month_resolved = tickets * resolved_loop
    point = 0.01  # one point of automated acceptance
    point_value = point * c_human  # fallback spend avoided per ticket

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(
        all(0 < p < 1 for p in (p_rules, p_call, r1, r2, r3, human_resolution, resolution_floor)),
        "Scenario probabilities lie strictly between zero and one",
    )
    check(abs(p_loop - (r1 + reach2 * r2 + reach3 * r3)) < 1e-12, "Mutually exclusive first-acceptance paths reconcile")
    check(1 < turns < 3, "Early stopping respects the three-turn cap")
    check(resolved_rules < resolution_floor <= resolved_call < resolved_loop, "Direct call and loop meet the declared combined resolution floor")
    check(0 * USD < per_loop < per_call < per_rules, "Loop is cheapest per combined resolution in this scenario")
    check(auto_per_rules < auto_per_loop < auto_per_call, "Automation-only cost ranking differs from combined-policy ranking")
    check(point_value > 5 * max(auto_rules, auto_call, auto_loop), "Fallback dominates automated spend")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    tickets_str = fmt_int(tickets)
    c_rules_str = fmt_usd(c_rules, precision=3)
    c_call_str = fmt_usd(c_call, precision=3)
    c_turn_str = fmt_usd(c_turn, precision=3)
    c_ver_str = fmt_usd(c_ver, precision=3)
    c_human_str = fmt_usd(c_human, precision=0)
    human_resolution_str = fmt_percent(human_resolution, precision=0, style="prose")
    floor_str = fmt_percent(resolution_floor, precision=0, style="prose")
    p_rules_str = fmt_percent(p_rules, precision=0, style="prose")
    p_call_str = fmt_percent(p_call, precision=0, style="prose")
    r1_str = fmt(r1, precision=2)
    r2_str = fmt(r2, precision=2)
    r3_str = fmt(r3, precision=2)
    p_loop_str = fmt_percent(p_loop, precision=2, style="prose")
    turns_str = fmt(turns, precision=3)
    auto_rules_str = fmt_usd(auto_rules, precision=3)
    auto_call_str = fmt_usd(auto_call, precision=3)
    auto_loop_str = fmt_usd(auto_loop, precision=6)
    auto_per_rules_str = fmt_usd(auto_per_rules, precision=5)
    auto_per_call_str = fmt_usd(auto_per_call, precision=5)
    auto_per_loop_str = fmt_usd(auto_per_loop, precision=5)
    resolved_rules_str = fmt_percent(resolved_rules, precision=3, style="symbol")
    resolved_call_str = fmt_percent(resolved_call, precision=3, style="symbol")
    resolved_loop_str = fmt_percent(resolved_loop, precision=3, style="symbol")
    total_rules_str = fmt_usd(total_rules, precision=3)
    total_call_str = fmt_usd(total_call, precision=3)
    total_loop_str = fmt_usd(total_loop, precision=6)
    per_rules_str = fmt_usd(per_rules, precision=2)
    per_call_str = fmt_usd(per_call, precision=2)
    per_loop_str = fmt_usd(per_loop, precision=2)
    month_loop_str = fmt_usd(month_loop, precision=2)
    month_resolved_str = fmt(month_resolved, precision=1)
    point_value_str = fmt_usd(point_value, precision=2)
```

::: {#nbk-18-architectural-frontier-migration-under-cost .callout-notebook title="Pricing three designs for dependency upgrades"}

**Problem**: A team expects `{python} ArchitectureChoice.tickets_str` dependency-upgrade tickets per month. Each requires edits that pass the same declared build and regression assessment. A rule-based rewriter costs `{python} ArchitectureChoice.c_rules_str` before assessment and achieves automated acceptance on `{python} ArchitectureChoice.p_rules_str` of tickets. A single model call costs `{python} ArchitectureChoice.c_call_str` before assessment and accepts `{python} ArchitectureChoice.p_call_str`. A cheaper model loop costs `{python} ArchitectureChoice.c_turn_str` per reached turn before assessment, stops after acceptance or three turns, and has conditional acceptance probabilities `{python} ArchitectureChoice.r1_str`, `{python} ArchitectureChoice.r2_str`, and `{python} ArchitectureChoice.r3_str`. Every automated candidate incurs the same `{python} ArchitectureChoice.c_ver_str` assessment charge. Other automated prices include model or program execution, runtime, sandbox holding, and cleanup under the stipulated operating conditions. One human fallback on each automated rejection costs `{python} ArchitectureChoice.c_human_str`, including final assessment and all remaining handling, and resolves `{python} ArchitectureChoice.human_resolution_str` of those tickets. Under these hypothetical population expectations, which design minimizes cost per resolved ticket while achieving at least `{python} ArchitectureChoice.floor_str` combined resolution?

**Math**: By @eq-vol3-loop-success the loop accepts `{python} ArchitectureChoice.p_loop_str` automatically and executes `{python} ArchitectureChoice.turns_str` turns on average. The separate accounts in @tbl-vol3-architecture-decision prevent human completions from appearing as automated successes.

| Expected quantity                                     |                                         Rewriter |                                     Single call |                                    Bounded loop |
|:------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------:|------------------------------------------------:|------------------------------------------------:|
| Automated spend per incoming ticket, including checks |     `{python} ArchitectureChoice.auto_rules_str` |     `{python} ArchitectureChoice.auto_call_str` |     `{python} ArchitectureChoice.auto_loop_str` |
| Automated spend per automated acceptance              | `{python} ArchitectureChoice.auto_per_rules_str` | `{python} ArchitectureChoice.auto_per_call_str` | `{python} ArchitectureChoice.auto_per_loop_str` |
| Resolution probability, including human fallback      | `{python} ArchitectureChoice.resolved_rules_str` | `{python} ArchitectureChoice.resolved_call_str` | `{python} ArchitectureChoice.resolved_loop_str` |
| Combined spend per incoming ticket                    |    `{python} ArchitectureChoice.total_rules_str` |    `{python} ArchitectureChoice.total_call_str` |    `{python} ArchitectureChoice.total_loop_str` |
| Combined spend per resolved ticket                    |      `{python} ArchitectureChoice.per_rules_str` |      `{python} ArchitectureChoice.per_call_str` |      `{python} ArchitectureChoice.per_loop_str` |

: **Dependency-Upgrade Decision Account**: Expected spend includes rejected attempts and unsuccessful human fallback; the automated and combined denominators represent different outcomes. {#tbl-vol3-architecture-decision}

**Systems insight**: When a human fallback follows every rejection, automated acceptance dominates the account. Each point of acceptance avoids `{python} ArchitectureChoice.point_value_str` of fallback per ticket, several times any design's entire automated spend, so the rewriter's lowest cost per automated acceptance still leaves it the most expensive design per resolved ticket and below the resolution floor. The loop wins because its second and third turns convert rejections that would otherwise reach a person. Its projected monthly spend is `{python} ArchitectureChoice.month_loop_str` for `{python} ArchitectureChoice.month_resolved_str` expected resolved tickets, an expectation rather than an observed count. The ranking follows from the stipulated conditional acceptance rates and fallback cost, which a real decision measures.

:::

The calculation assumes completed assessments and settled charges; an observed evaluation keeps pending verdicts and outstanding work visible at its cutoff and counts every initiated attempt. Human resolution uses the same task contract. The example leaves queueing, completion-time distributions, and reviewer capacity unmeasured, so a deadline or staffing limit can overturn its choice.

Delegation follows the same objective-first comparison against a capable single controller (@sec-vol3-multiagent-evaluation). A more expensive design is worthwhile when it meets a deadline the cheaper design misses; Pareto dominance is sufficient but not required.

## Cost per Accepted Task by Archetype {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-synthesis}

The dependency-upgrade comparison priced three designs for one workload. The four lighthouse workloads introduced in @sec-vol3-intro put the same account under different pressure: the repair agent carries a growing workspace context, the research agent (\ref{lhs-vol3-research-agent}) fans out over untrusted sources, the remediation agent (\ref{lhs-vol3-remediation-agent}) holds authority over production state, and the support agent (\ref{lhs-vol3-support-agent}) answers many short sessions against a deadline. Each has a different largest term in its attempt cost, so each rewards a different lever from this chapter.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-lighthouses
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COST PER ACCEPTED TASK BY ARCHETYPE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @lhs-18-cost-per-accepted-by-archetype and @tbl-vol3-lighthouse-economics.
# │ Goal: Price one attempt for each of the four lighthouse workloads.
# │ Show: C_eff per workload and its response to three levers.
# │ How:  C_eff = C_attempt / p_acc; the support handoff scales with (1 - p_acc).
# │ Note: Repair horizon from the registry harness and repair token bill from
# │       PrefixCacheCost. Research, remediation, and support inputs come from
# │       the Agents.Research/Remediation/Support workload profiles; only the
# │       research fan-out multiple is sourced (anthropic2025multiagent), and
# │       every other input is a documented teaching value, not a measurement.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Agents, USD
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_usd

def _usd(q):
    """Magnitude in USD of a registry currency quantity."""
    return q.to(USD).magnitude

class LighthouseEconomics:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Registry, cross-cell, cited, and scenario inputs) ─────────
    # Repair agent: horizon capped by the registry's reference coding harness;
    # its token bill is the append-only trajectory priced in PrefixCacheCost.
    repair_turns = Agents.Coding.SWE_Bench_Runner.max_trajectory_steps
    repair_model = PrefixCacheCost.total_cache.to(USD).magnitude
    repair_env_per_turn = 0.03  # scenario USD: sandbox holding and tool use per turn
    repair_assess = 0.10  # scenario USD: sealed regression suite per attempt
    repair_p = 0.40  # scenario acceptance probability
    # Research agent: orchestrator-worker fan-out over web sources.
    research = Agents.Research.OrchestratorWorker
    research_turns = research.horizon_turns
    chat_in = research.chat_input_tokens.to("token").magnitude  # one single-chat answer
    chat_out = research.chat_output_tokens.to("token").magnitude
    fanout_multiple = research.fanout_token_multiple  # ~15x chat tokens (anthropic2025multiagent)
    research_env = _usd(research.environment_cost_per_attempt)  # search and fetch fees
    research_assess = _usd(research.assessment_cost_per_attempt)  # rubric grader per report
    research_p = research.acceptance_probability
    # Remediation agent: one approved production change per attempt.
    remediation = Agents.Remediation.OnCall
    remediation_turns = remediation.horizon_turns
    remediation_model = _usd(remediation.model_cost_per_attempt)
    remediation_env = _usd(remediation.environment_cost_per_attempt)  # observability queries, change tools
    remediation_assess = _usd(remediation.assessment_cost_per_attempt)  # post-change health-check window
    remediation_p = remediation.acceptance_probability
    # Support agent: one customer session per attempt.
    support = Agents.Support.CustomerOps
    support_turns = support.horizon_turns
    support_model = _usd(support.model_cost_per_attempt)
    support_env = _usd(support.environment_cost_per_attempt)  # customer-record lookups
    support_assess = _usd(support.assessment_cost_per_attempt)  # policy-grounding check
    handoff = _usd(support.handoff_cost)  # human pick-up cost per rejected session
    support_p = support.acceptance_probability
    dp = 0.10  # acceptance lever: absolute gain in acceptance probability

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Attempt cost, C_eff, and three levers) ────────────────
    chat_cost = ((chat_in * PrefixCacheCost.p_in + chat_out * PrefixCacheCost.p_out) / 1_000_000).to(USD).magnitude
    research_model = fanout_multiple * chat_cost
    repair_env = repair_turns * repair_env_per_turn
    remediation_human = _usd(remediation.approval_cost_per_attempt)  # reviewer time x hourly rate
    support_human = (1 - support_p) * handoff
    model = (repair_model, research_model, remediation_model, support_model)
    env = (repair_env, research_env, remediation_env, support_env)
    assess = (repair_assess, research_assess, remediation_assess, support_assess)
    human = (0.0, 0.0, remediation_human, support_human)
    p_acc = (repair_p, research_p, remediation_p, support_p)
    attempt, ceff, share, save_tok, save_big, save_acc = [], [], [], [], [], []
    for j in range(4):
        a_j = model[j] + env[j] + assess[j] + human[j]
        c_j = a_j / p_acc[j]
        big_j = max(model[j], env[j], assess[j], human[j])
        p2_j = p_acc[j] + dp
        # Support's handoff is charged per rejected session, so it falls with p.
        h2_j = (1 - p2_j) * handoff if j == 3 else human[j]
        attempt.append(a_j)
        ceff.append(c_j)
        share.append(model[j] / a_j)
        save_tok.append(1 - (a_j - model[j] / 2) / p_acc[j] / c_j)
        save_big.append(1 - (a_j - big_j / 2) / p_acc[j] / c_j)
        save_acc.append(1 - (a_j - human[j] + h2_j) / p2_j / c_j)
    repair_threshold = 2 * dp / (repair_p + dp)  # model share below which acceptance wins

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants and the decision rule) ───────────────────────
    check(repair_turns == PrefixCacheCost.turns, "Repair token bill must span the registry horizon")
    for j in range(3):
        check(abs(save_tok[j] - share[j] / 2) < 1e-12, "Halving tokens saves half the model share")
        check(abs(save_acc[j] - dp / (p_acc[j] + dp)) < 1e-12, "Acceptance saves dp/(p+dp) of every term")
    check(share[0] < repair_threshold and save_acc[0] > save_tok[0], "Repair: acceptance beats token price")
    check(save_tok[1] == save_big[1] and save_tok[1] > save_acc[1], "Research: tokens are the largest term and the lever")
    check(save_tok[2] < 0.01 and save_big[2] > 0.4, "Remediation: approval dominates")
    check(save_acc[3] > save_big[3] > save_tok[3], "Support: acceptance also removes handoffs")
    check(ceff[3] < 1 < ceff[1] < ceff[0] < ceff[2], "Scenario ordering of C_eff")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    repair_turns_str, research_turns_str = fmt_int(repair_turns), fmt_int(research_turns)
    remediation_turns_str, support_turns_str = fmt_int(remediation_turns), fmt_int(support_turns)
    fanout_mult_str = fmt_multiple(fanout_multiple, precision=0)
    repair_model_str, research_model_str, remediation_model_str, support_model_str = (fmt_usd(x, precision=2) for x in model)
    repair_env_str, research_env_str, remediation_env_str, support_env_str = (fmt_usd(x, precision=2) for x in env)
    repair_assess_str, research_assess_str, remediation_assess_str, support_assess_str = (fmt_usd(x, precision=2) for x in assess)
    repair_human_str, research_human_str, remediation_human_str, support_human_str = (
        fmt_usd(x, precision=0 if abs(x - round(x)) < 1e-9 else 2) for x in human
    )
    repair_attempt_str, research_attempt_str, remediation_attempt_str, support_attempt_str = (fmt_usd(x, precision=2) for x in attempt)
    repair_p_str, research_p_str, remediation_p_str, support_p_str = (fmt(x, precision=2) for x in p_acc)
    repair_ceff_str, research_ceff_str, remediation_ceff_str, support_ceff_str = (fmt_usd(x, precision=2) for x in ceff)
    repair_tok_str, research_tok_str, remediation_tok_str, support_tok_str = (
        fmt_percent(x, precision=0 if abs(100 * x - round(100 * x)) < 1e-9 else 1, style="symbol") for x in save_tok
    )
    repair_big_str, research_big_str, remediation_big_str, support_big_str = (
        fmt_percent(x, precision=0 if abs(100 * x - round(100 * x)) < 1e-9 else 1, style="symbol") for x in save_big
    )
    repair_acc_str, research_acc_str, remediation_acc_str, support_acc_str = (
        fmt_percent(x, precision=0 if abs(100 * x - round(100 * x)) < 1e-9 else 1, style="symbol") for x in save_acc
    )
    repair_share_str = fmt_percent(share[0], precision=1, style="prose")
    research_share_str = fmt_percent(share[1], precision=1, style="prose")
    repair_threshold_str = fmt_percent(repair_threshold, precision=0, style="prose")
    handoff_str = fmt_usd(handoff, precision=0)
    dp_pts_str = fmt_int(round(dp * 100))
```

::: {#lhs-18-cost-per-accepted-by-archetype .callout-lighthouse title="Cost per accepted task by archetype"}

Each lighthouse runs one attempt under its own acceptance contract, and @tbl-vol3-lighthouse-economics prices it with the chapter's account. The repair agent's horizon is the step cap of the registry's reference coding harness, and its token bill is the cached append-only trajectory of notebook \ref{nbk-18-prefix-cache-dollars}. The research agent's token bill applies the `{python} LighthouseEconomics.fanout_mult_str` multiple of chat tokens that one 2025 engineering account reported for a production multi-agent research system [@anthropic2025multiagent], a point-in-time measurement rather than a constant, to one single-chat answer at the same tariff. The remediation agent pays an on-call engineer to approve its production change, and each rejected support session hands off to a human agent at `{python} LighthouseEconomics.handoff_str`. All other inputs are scenario values.

| Quantity                                                                        |                                      Repair agent |                                      Research agent |                                      Remediation agent |                                      Support agent |
|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------:|----------------------------------------------------:|-------------------------------------------------------:|---------------------------------------------------:|
| Horizon (turns)                                                                 |   `{python} LighthouseEconomics.repair_turns_str` |   `{python} LighthouseEconomics.research_turns_str` |   `{python} LighthouseEconomics.remediation_turns_str` |   `{python} LighthouseEconomics.support_turns_str` |
| Model tokens                                                                    |   `{python} LighthouseEconomics.repair_model_str` |   `{python} LighthouseEconomics.research_model_str` |   `{python} LighthouseEconomics.remediation_model_str` |   `{python} LighthouseEconomics.support_model_str` |
| Sandbox, tools, and services                                                    |     `{python} LighthouseEconomics.repair_env_str` |     `{python} LighthouseEconomics.research_env_str` |     `{python} LighthouseEconomics.remediation_env_str` |     `{python} LighthouseEconomics.support_env_str` |
| Assessment                                                                      |  `{python} LighthouseEconomics.repair_assess_str` |  `{python} LighthouseEconomics.research_assess_str` |  `{python} LighthouseEconomics.remediation_assess_str` |  `{python} LighthouseEconomics.support_assess_str` |
| Human work (approval or expected handoff)                                       |   `{python} LighthouseEconomics.repair_human_str` |   `{python} LighthouseEconomics.research_human_str` |   `{python} LighthouseEconomics.remediation_human_str` |   `{python} LighthouseEconomics.support_human_str` |
| **Attempt cost**                                                                | `{python} LighthouseEconomics.repair_attempt_str` | `{python} LighthouseEconomics.research_attempt_str` | `{python} LighthouseEconomics.remediation_attempt_str` | `{python} LighthouseEconomics.support_attempt_str` |
| Acceptance probability                                                          |       `{python} LighthouseEconomics.repair_p_str` |       `{python} LighthouseEconomics.research_p_str` |       `{python} LighthouseEconomics.remediation_p_str` |       `{python} LighthouseEconomics.support_p_str` |
| **Cost per accepted task**                                                      |    `{python} LighthouseEconomics.repair_ceff_str` |    `{python} LighthouseEconomics.research_ceff_str` |    `{python} LighthouseEconomics.remediation_ceff_str` |    `{python} LighthouseEconomics.support_ceff_str` |
