| Largest term                                                                    |                                 Sandbox and tests |                                      Fan-out tokens |                                         Human approval |                                 Escalation handoff |
| Saving from halving the token price                                             |     `{python} LighthouseEconomics.repair_tok_str` |     `{python} LighthouseEconomics.research_tok_str` |     `{python} LighthouseEconomics.remediation_tok_str` |     `{python} LighthouseEconomics.support_tok_str` |
| Saving from halving the largest term                                            |     `{python} LighthouseEconomics.repair_big_str` |     `{python} LighthouseEconomics.research_big_str` |     `{python} LighthouseEconomics.remediation_big_str` |     `{python} LighthouseEconomics.support_big_str` |
| Saving from `{python} LighthouseEconomics.dp_pts_str` more points of acceptance |     `{python} LighthouseEconomics.repair_acc_str` |     `{python} LighthouseEconomics.research_acc_str` |     `{python} LighthouseEconomics.remediation_acc_str` |     `{python} LighthouseEconomics.support_acc_str` |

: **Cost per Accepted Task by Archetype**: One attempt per lighthouse workload under the chapter's tariff. Savings are reductions in cost per accepted task. Only the repair horizon (registry) and the research fan-out multiple (cited report) come from outside the scenario; every other value is an assumed input, not a measurement. {#tbl-vol3-lighthouse-economics}

**Systems insight**: Halving the token price saves half of the model's share of the attempt, while raising acceptance from $p$ to $p+\Delta p$ saves the fraction $\Delta p/(p+\Delta p)$ of every term. Acceptance is therefore the better lever whenever the model's share is below $2\Delta p/(p+\Delta p)$, which is `{python} LighthouseEconomics.repair_threshold_str` for the repair agent, whose tokens are `{python} LighthouseEconomics.repair_share_str` of its attempt. Only the research agent, whose tokens are `{python} LighthouseEconomics.research_share_str` of its attempt, is bound by token price, which makes caching, compaction, and bounded fan-out its levers. The repair agent is bound by sandbox and test time, the same interval the critical-path analysis found; the remediation agent by human approval, which approval escrow (@sec-vol3-agent-harness) and batching of reversible actions reduce, with its expected irreversible loss (@sec-vol3-failure-recovery) on top; and the support agent by escalation, whose handoff charge falls with every point of acceptance. The support agent's cost per accepted task is under a dollar, so its binding constraint is capacity rather than cost: time to first token across many concurrent sessions, sized with the queueing arithmetic of @sec-vol3-agent-economics-capacity.

:::

For any one workload, the decision record keeps the comparison's accounting boundary when it becomes an operating report: failed and canceled work, shared capacity with its idle reserve, human work inside the contract, and pending outcomes and outstanding liabilities at the cutoff. That boundary lets the ranking be re-tested when the workload changes. A cheaper model, a harder mix of tasks, or a new approval policy reopens the matched comparison, and a policy that wins on paper earns a loaded service only after its test, sandbox, and reviewer capacity have been measured at the intended admission rate.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-fallacies}

An economic comparison can be arithmetically correct while counting the wrong work or accepting a different outcome. These mistakes occur when a component's price, speed, or stopping condition replaces the trajectory-level account.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-agent-economics-fallacies
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PRICING THE FALLACIES AND PITFALLS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-agent-economics-fallacies.
# │ Goal: Price the cached-read share and the false-accept break-even of the cascade.
# │ Show: Share of the cached bill still spent re-reading history; tier-1
# │       false-accept rate at which remediation erases the cascade's saving.
# │ How:  Reads PrefixCacheCost and CascadeCost; one scenario harm per false accept.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import USD
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_percent, fmt_usd

class EconomicsFallacies:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Earlier cells and one scenario harm) ─────────────────────
    sent, fresh = PrefixCacheCost.sent, PrefixCacheCost.fresh
    cached_share, p_in = PrefixCacheCost.cached_share, PrefixCacheCost.p_in
    total_cache = PrefixCacheCost.total_cache
    first_tier_exits = CascadeCost.accepted_by_tier[0]
    accepted, per_accepted = CascadeCost.accepted, CascadeCost.per_accepted
    direct_per_accepted = CascadeCost.direct_per_accepted
    harm = 10.0  # scenario USD to find and remediate one falsely accepted edit

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Cached re-read share; cascade harm break-even) ────────
    cached_reads = cached_share * (sent - fresh) * p_in / 1_000_000
    reread_share = (cached_reads / total_cache).to(USD / USD).magnitude
    saving_per_accepted = direct_per_accepted - per_accepted
    fa_breakeven = saving_per_accepted * accepted / (first_tier_exits * harm)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0.4 < reread_share < 0.6, "Cached re-reads remain about half the cached bill")
    check(0 < fa_breakeven < 0.02, "A small tier-1 false-accept rate erases the saving")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    reread_share_str = fmt_percent(reread_share, precision=0 if abs(100 * reread_share - round(100 * reread_share)) < 1e-9 else 1)
    harm_str = fmt_usd(harm, precision=0)
    saving_per_accepted_str = fmt_usd(saving_per_accepted, precision=3)
    fa_breakeven_str = fmt_percent(fa_breakeven, precision=1)
```

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy:** *The lowest token price identifies the cheapest accepted task.*

A lower rate is offset by longer contexts, additional turns, tool use, assessment, and human handling, all divided by acceptance. In notebook \ref{nbk-18-the-token-price-fallacy-in-automated}, the low-price configuration cuts token charges by `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.model_cut_str` percent and each attempt by `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.attempt_cut_str` percent, yet costs `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.eff_ratio_mult_str` as much per accepted repair, and `{python} TokenPriceFallacy.eff_h_ratio_mult_str` once triage of rejected attempts enters the account. Compare total initiated-work cost with the accepted count under the same contract (@sec-vol3-agent-economics-accounting).
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall:** *Buying faster generation without identifying what delays completion.*

A faster model shortens only the model's share of elapsed time. In the serial repair episode of notebook \ref{nbk-18-critical-path-investment}, a `{python} CriticalPath.model_speedup_mult_str` model speedup saves `{python} CriticalPath.saving_str` of `{python} CriticalPath.total_str`, a `{python} CriticalPath.speedup_mult_str` gain, and instantaneous model calls would stop at `{python} CriticalPath.limiting_speedup_mult_str`; halving the test interval would save `{python} CriticalPath.tests_half_saving_str`. Locate the completion path from nonoverlapping durations and actual dependencies first, including queueing and idle intervals, then price the intervention under the intended load (@sec-vol3-agent-economics-criticalpath).
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy:** *Prefix caching makes carried context nearly free.*

Caching lowers the coefficient of the quadratic re-read term; it does not remove it. In notebook \ref{nbk-18-prefix-cache-dollars}, ideal reuse cuts the token bill by `{python} PrefixCacheCost.cache_ratio_mult_str`, yet re-reading cached history is still `{python} EconomicsFallacies.reread_share_str` percent of what remains, and it keeps growing with the square of the horizon. The saving also depends on the hit rate: losing `{python} PrefixCacheCost.hit_drop_str` percent of eligible hits raises the cached bill by `{python} PrefixCacheCost.miss_pct_str` percent. Keep the prefix stable, and compact early enough to repay the rebuild (@sec-vol3-agent-economics-caching).
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall:** *Running shared model capacity near saturation to lower its unit cost.*

Utilization buys throughput linearly and costs waiting hyperbolically. In notebook \ref{nbk-18-sizing-queue-capacity-and-tail}, moving from `{python} QueuePrice.rho_low_str` to `{python} QueuePrice.rho_high_str` utilization adds `{python} QueuePrice.throughput_gain_str` of throughput and multiplies mean wait by `{python} QueuePrice.wait_ratio_mult_str`. A trajectory pays that wait on every serial call, and with `{python} TailCompounding.n_calls_str` calls it meets at least one per-call tail delay with probability `{python} TailCompounding.p_hit_str`. Size reserve against trajectory-level percentiles, not per-call means (@sec-vol3-agent-economics-capacity).
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy:** *A cascade's cheap first tier makes its savings independent of its gate.*

The cascade in notebook \ref{nbk-18-cost-and-latency-trade-offs-in} saves `{python} EconomicsFallacies.saving_per_accepted_str` per accepted result over direct execution only because every exit meets the same contract. If a cheaper tier-1 gate falsely accepted `{python} EconomicsFallacies.fa_breakeven_str` percent of its exits, and each false acceptance cost `{python} EconomicsFallacies.harm_str` to find and repair, the harm term would erase the entire saving. Price gate costs, escalation, unresolved outcomes, and false-accept harm together, and keep the contract fixed across tiers (@sec-vol3-agent-economics-cascades).
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall:** *Returning a canceled child's unused-looking allowance to the spending pool at local stop.*

Local termination can precede remote settlement. In notebook \ref{nbk-18-hierarchical-multi-agent-budget-allocation-and}, a release at stop would have returned `{python} BudgetLedger.fuzz_apparent_free_str` when only `{python} BudgetLedger.fuzz_free_at_stop_str` was free, and the `{python} BudgetLedger.late_charge_str` late bill would have landed on funds already promised to a sibling. Release only the allocation minus settled charges minus enforceable bounds on outstanding work; atomic admission and idempotent settlement keep siblings and duplicate billing records from reusing the same allowance, and a retrospective burn-rate alert cannot supply that guarantee (@sec-vol3-agent-economics-governance).
:::

## Summary {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-summary}

Economics connects the work a system initiates to the outcome it is intended to deliver. Per-attempt cost records what execution consumes; cost per accepted task, $C_{\text{eff}}$, charges the complete cohort to its accepted results, so acceptance divides every term while a token discount moves only one. The objective, deadline, authority constraints, and scope of the assessment decide which trade-offs are admissible.

The chapter's decisions build on that account. Caching, compaction, and retry policies change what is purchased; critical-path analysis finds where faster execution can matter; routing changes which capabilities are tried; capacity planning prices the resources held and the waits that concurrent work imposes; and spending governance makes the resulting commitments enforceable. Priced across the four lighthouse workloads, the same account names a different lever for each: tokens for the research agent, sandbox and test time for the repair agent, approval for the remediation agent, and acceptance and serving capacity for the support agent.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Price the accepted task, not the token"}

* **Keep the cost boundary and outcome population together**: Count all initiated work, including failed and canceled attempts, assessment, cleanup, and human work within the boundary. Distinguish per-attempt cost from cost per accepted task, and retain pending verdicts and charges explicitly.
* **Price reuse and additional attempts under their actual contracts**: Cache validity and billing determine savings; compaction adds summary and possible rebuild costs. Retry purchases depend on the stopping and assessment policy, not an assumption that every additional attempt is independent or useful.
* **Invest where the completion path can change**: Trace dependencies and nonoverlapping work rather than summing nested spans. Evaluate acceleration under the intended load, preserving required evidence even when tests or observations are shortened.
* **Hold the acceptance contract fixed across routes and designs**: Price each reached model and gate, escalation, and unresolved outcomes under one contract. Where human fallback follows rejection, each point of automated acceptance can be worth more than the entire automated spend.
* **Size each resource for its own occupancy**: Trajectory concurrency, call service, and quota demand are different quantities, and a drop in acceptance raises all three for the same goodput. Waiting grows as $\rho/(1-\rho)$, so reserve is sized against trajectory-level percentiles; compare capacity sources under equivalent task capability.
* **Reserve liability before admitting work**: Atomic, durable ledger transitions conserve allocated funds across descendants. Settle each operation once, preserve backing for late charges, and distinguish enforceable admission limits from retrospective spending signals.
* **Find the workload's largest term before choosing a lever**: Halving the token price saves half the model's share; raising acceptance saves a fraction of every term. The four lighthouse workloads are bound by different terms, so the same intervention can save nearly half the cost of one and almost nothing of another.

:::

Trajectory goodput and the accepted task (principle \ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-goodput}) acquire an explicit financial account, $C_{\text{eff}}$, and its reciprocal, goodput per dollar, and the same principle requires the account to include resource residence and waiting, not just active generation. Trajectory-level encapsulation (principle \ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}) preserves spending responsibility across children through reservations and settlement, while leaving reusable permissions distinct from consumable funds.

## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-vol3-agent-economics-history}

The time and capacity half of this chapter's account is operations research from the mid-twentieth century. Project planners needed to know which activities fixed a completion date, and the critical-path method answered with the longest chain of dependent work [@kelley1959critical]. Queueing theory supplied the capacity laws: Little proved that mean occupancy equals arrival rate times mean residence under very general conditions [@little1961], and Kingman showed in the same year that a single server's waiting time grows without bound, in proportion to $1/(1-\rho)$, as load approaches one [@kingman1961single], results later consolidated in textbook form [@kleinrock1975queueing]. When parallel computers promised large speedups, Amdahl's fixed-work argument bounded what accelerating one part of a job could buy [@amdahl1967]. Each generation hit the same problem the repair agent hits, a fast component inside a slow whole, and answered it by accounting for the whole.

The spending half descends from transaction processing and utility computing. Databases that had to update hot account balances under heavy concurrency learned to escrow part of a quantity instead of locking it [@oneil1986escrow], within a broader discipline of atomic, durable, recoverable updates [@gray1992]. When computing capacity became rentable by the hour, the argument for renting over owning turned on average utilization and on who bears the risk of provisioning [@armbrust2010view], and warehouse-scale services learned that rare per-request delays dominate once a request touches many servers [@dean2013tail].

Machine learning brought its own lineage of paying for computation only where it is needed. A boosted classifier cascade made real-time detection possible by discarding easy cases early [@viola2001], and the same shape returned for language model APIs as cascades and learned routers [@chen2023frugalgpt; @ong2024routellm]. Draft-then-verify decoding grew from blockwise parallel prediction [@stern2018blockwise] into speculative decoding [@leviathan2023fast; @chen2023accelerating]. Repeated sampling showed that more attempts keep buying coverage when a check can recognize success [@brown2024monkeys], and that result made the question this chapter answers unavoidable: evaluations of agents had to report what the accuracy cost [@kapoor2024agents].

**Further reading.**

- *The Single Server Queue in Heavy Traffic* [@kingman1961single]. Three pages that explain why waiting, not throughput, is the price of high utilization.
- *The Escrow Transactional Method* [@oneil1986escrow]. The database ancestor of budget reservations, showing how concurrent work can share one bounded quantity without a global lock.
- *A View of Cloud Computing* [@armbrust2010view]. The utilization and risk-transfer argument behind every rent-versus-own decision, including per-token APIs.
- *Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems* [@harchol-balter2013]. The queueing models this chapter deliberately stops short of, including multiple servers, variability, and scheduling policy.
- *The Tail at Scale* [@dean2013tail]. Why systems must be engineered against percentiles rather than means once work is composed of many calls.
- *AI Agents That Matter* [@kapoor2024agents]. The case for reporting agent accuracy and cost together, which is the evaluation counterpart of cost per accepted task.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ End-to-end integration, trajectory ownership, and specification boundaries are synthesized in @sec-vol3-conclusion.
:::

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From priced parts to one trajectory"}

Who owns each transition between context, tools, execution, assessment, and settlement, and what evidence permits the next one? An economically justified policy still crosses all of those boundaries. @Sec-vol3-conclusion follows those responsibilities through one trajectory and examines failures at their seams. It then returns to the specification boundary: the runtime can enforce and measure a declared contract, but those mechanisms do not decide whether the contract captures what the task was for.

:::
